Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to explore the forest near her house. One day, she found a mushroom. It was big and red and looked so yummy. 

But Lily knew she had to be careful. She picked it up and examined it closely. She noticed it was very heavy and had lots of little bumps on it. 

Lily decided not to eat the mushroom, just in case it was dangerous. Instead, she took it home to show her mommy and daddy. They were very proud of her for being so smart and careful. 

From that day on, Lily always examined things before touching them. She knew it was important to be safe, especially when exploring the forest. And she never forgot about the heavy mushroom she found that day.

Tom and Mia liked to play with blocks. They liked to make towers and houses and bridges. Sometimes they made a game of who could make the highest tower. They used all the blocks they had.

One day, they saw a new box of blocks in the corner. It was big and shiny and had a picture of a giant on it. Tom and Mia wanted to see what was inside. They opened the box and found many big and colorful blocks. They were very happy.

"Let's use these blocks to make our towers," Tom said.

"Yes, let's," Mia agreed.

They took the blocks and started to add them to their towers. They made them taller and taller and taller. They did not notice that the box had a label that said: "Do not open. These blocks belong to Ben."

Ben was their big brother. He was six years old and he liked to build things too. He had saved his money to buy the box of blocks. He had hidden it in the corner until he could find a good place to play with it. He was at school when Tom and Mia opened his box.

When he came home, he saw his box was open and his blocks were gone. He looked around and saw Tom and Mia's towers. They had used his blocks. He was very angry.

"Hey, those are my blocks!" he shouted. "You took them without asking. That's not fair."

Tom and Mia heard Ben's voice and felt guilty. They knew they had done something wrong. They looked at their towers and then at Ben. They did not know what to say.

"We're sorry, Ben," Mia said. "We didn't know they were yours. We just wanted to play."

"Yeah, we're sorry," Tom said. "We thought they were for everyone. We didn't mean to make you mad."

Ben looked at them and saw they were sorry. He was still angry, but he also loved his brother and sister. He decided to be nice.

"It's okay, I guess," he said. "But next time, you have to ask before you use something that's not yours. And you have to share."

"Okay, we will," Tom and Mia said.

"Can we play with your blocks, please?" Mia asked.

"Sure, you can," Ben said. "But only if I can play with you."

"Okay, you can," Tom and Mia said.

They smiled and hugged Ben. Then they all played with the blocks together. They made a giant tower that reached the ceiling. They had fun.

LILY-GIRL, not made for this world's pain, With brown, soft hair close braided by her ears, And longing eyes half veiled by slumberous tears Like bluest water seen through mists of rain: Pale cheeks whereon no love hath left its stain, Red underlip drawn in for fear of love, And white throat, whiter than the silvered dove, Through whose wan marble creeps one purple vein. Yet, though my lips shall praise her without cease, Even to kiss her feet I am not bold, Being o'ershadowed by the wings of awe, Like Dante, when he stood with Beatrice Beneath the flaming Lion's breast, and saw The seventh Crystal, and the Stair of Gold

Once upon a time in a little town there was a little hedge. One day, a small yellow bird came and sat on the hedge. She looked around and saw a big hill. The bird saw something very exciting. She saw a zip! It was a zip line! The bird was so little and she was very curious. She wanted to try it out. The bird flapped her wings and flew up to the zip line. She hopped on and grabbed onto the rope. Then, she zipped all the way down the hill. She had so much fun zipping down the hill that she flew around the little town, zipping in the sky. The little bird loved zipping around the town and very often she would zip down the same hill, just for fun.

One day there was an iron in the garden. It was very graceful and shiny. One day, a big strong wind came and it made the iron break. Everyone was sad and they didn't know how to fix it.

Then a butterfly came and it flew gracefully around the iron. The butterfly waved its wings around the iron and said some magical words. Miraculously, the iron started to come back together and it was as good as new. Everyone was amazed and they clapped their hands in delight.

From then on, the iron was a symbol of hope and grace in the garden. Whenever anyone saw it, they remembered the power of grace and the gust of wind that had made it break.

Once there was a little girl named Sarah. She was walking in the woods when she heard someone shout. She thought it was a nice sound, so she followed it.

When Sarah got closer, she saw a crocodile. She was scared at first, but the crocodile smiled and it looked so peaceful. She sat down and began to talk to it.

The crocodile was so friendly and seemed like it wanted to play! He shouted and asked Sarah to join him in a game.

Sarah got so excited and started to play with the crocodile. She threw a stick, and the crocodile chased after it. She ran after the crocodile and they played until it was dark.

When it was time to go, Sarah was sad to leave the crocodile. She waved goodbye and went home, smiling from ear to ear.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to explore and play outside. One day, she decided to go on an adventure to a big mountain she saw in the distance. 

Lily walked and walked, but the mountain seemed to get farther and farther away. She was tired, but she was persistent and didn't give up. Finally, she reached the mountain and was amazed by its size. 

As she was looking at the mountain, a friendly bear walked up to her. "Hello there," said the bear. "My name is Benny. What are you doing here?" 

"I came to see the mountain," replied Lily. "It's very big!" 

"Yes, it is," said Benny. "I come here often. Would you like to climb it with me?" 

Lily was excited to meet a new friend and agreed to climb the mountain with Benny. They climbed and climbed until they reached the top. From there, they could see the whole world. Lily was so happy she decided to come on this adventure and meet Benny.

Once riding in old Baltimore, Heart-filled, head-filled with glee, I saw a Baltimorean Keep looking straight at me. Now I was eight and very small, And he was no whit bigger, And so I smiled, but he poked out His tongue, and called me, "Nigger." I saw the whole of Baltimore From May until December; Of all the things that happened there That's all that I remember.

name_of_work: Prayer Before Birth by Louis MacNeice
content: I am not yet born; O hear me. Let not the bloodsucking bat or the rat or the stoat or the club-footed ghoul come near me. I am not yet born, console me. I fear that the human race may with tall walls wall me, with strong drugs dope me, with wise lies lure me, on black racks rack me, in blood-baths roll me. I am not yet born; provide me With water to dandle me, grass to grow for me, trees to talk to me, sky to sing to me, birds and a white light in the back of my mind to guide me. I am not yet born; forgive me For the sins that in me the world shall commit, my words when they speak to me, my thoughts when they think me, my treason engendered by traitors beyond me, my life when they murder by means of my hands, my death when they live me. I am not yet born; rehearse me In the parts I must play and the cues I must take when old men lecture me, bureaucrats hector me, mountains frown at me, lovers laugh at me, the white waves call me to folly and the desert calls me to doom and the beggar refuses my gift and my children curse me. I am not yet born; O hear me, Let not the man who is beast or who thinks he is God come near me. I am not yet born; O fill me With strength against those who would freeze my humanity, would dragoon me into a lethal automaton, would make me a cog in a machine, a thing with one face, a thing, and against all those who would dissipate my entirety, would blow me like thistledown hither and thither or hither and thither like water held in the hands would spill me. Let them not make me a stone and let them not spill me. Otherwise kill me.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to sing and dance, but she was always afraid to perform in front of others. One day, her mom gave her a note that said, "You can do anything if you try!" Lily felt happy and decided to test herself by singing in front of her family.

At first, Lily was nervous and her voice shook. But then she remembered the note and kept singing. Her family clapped and cheered, and Lily felt proud of herself. She realized that being afraid was stupid and that she could do anything she set her mind to.

From that day on, Lily never let fear stop her from trying new things. She knew that even if she failed, she could always try again. And she always kept the note with her, as a reminder that she was capable of anything. The end.

Once there was a young girl named Elle. She was very playful and had a lot of energy.

One day, when Elle was playing outside, she noticed something shining in the grass. She went over and saw that it was a piece of gold! Elle could not believe her eyes.

Elle showed her gold to her parents. Her parents were very excited and they reminded Elle to always be careful with her new treasure. Elle promised that she would be very careful with her gold.

Elle kept her gold safe and showed it to her friends every day. She was very proud of her treasure, and her parents were always there to remind her to be careful.

Elle's gold was a special reminder of how young and adventurous she was. She was happy and excited to have such a valuable possession.

Once upon a time, there were two very best friends. One was called Daisy and the other was called Leo. One day, Daisy wanted to show Leo how much she loved him by offering something special. "Let me give you this olive," she said, reaching into a basket to take out a very special olive.

Leo was so excited! "Thanks, Daisy!" he said happily.

Daisy smiled back, but then she noticed something strange. As Leo had reached out to take the olive, Daisy had seen that he was being a bit clumsy. Olive juice had spilled out of the olive and onto Leo's shirt.

Daisy felt bad that Leo had ruined his shirt, so she offered to help. "I can clean it off for you," she said kindly.

Leo smiled, and gratefully accepted Daisy's offer. Daisy took the olive and carefully wiped the juice off of Leo's shirt. 

Once she was done, Daisy offered Leo the olive again, and this time he was extra careful not to spill it.

The two friends were happy, and decided to enjoy their special olive together.

Mia and Ben were playing in the park. They liked to run and jump and swing. They saw a big pond with many ducks and fish. Mia wanted to feed the ducks some bread. Ben wanted to dive in the pond and swim with the fish.

"No, Ben, you can't dive in the pond. It is too deep and cold. And the fish might bite you. And the ducks might peck you. And you might get wet and dirty. And Mommy will be angry. And you might get sick. And you might drown. And you might..." Mia said, sounding fearful.

"But I want to dive in the pond. It looks fun and cool. And the fish are pretty and friendly. And the ducks are cute and fluffy. And I have my swimsuit and towel. And Mommy won't mind. And I won't get sick. And I can swim. And I can..." Ben said, sounding excited.

They argued and argued. Mia tried to pull Ben away from the pond. Ben tried to push Mia away from the pond. They both got angry and sad. They both stopped talking and playing.

Then they saw a big, yellow daisy growing near the pond. It was bright and beautiful. It smelled sweet and fresh. It made them smile and forget their fight.

"Look, Ben, a daisy. Do you like daisies?" Mia asked, sounding friendly.

"Yes, Mia, I like daisies. Do you like daisies?" Ben asked, sounding friendly.

"Yes, Ben, I like daisies. Can we pick the daisy and share it?" Mia asked, sounding happy.

"Yes, Mia, we can pick the daisy and share it. Can we also hug and say sorry?" Ben asked, sounding happy.

"Yes, Ben, we can hug and say sorry. And we can also play together and have fun. And we can also feed the ducks and watch the fish. But we can't dive in the pond, okay?" Mia asked, sounding kind.

"Okay, Mia, we can't dive in the pond. But we can do everything else. And we can also be friends and love each other. And we can also be careful and safe. And we can also be happy and good. Okay?" Ben asked, sounding kind.

"Okay, Ben, okay. Let's go and pick the daisy. And let's go and play. And let's go and be friends. And let's go and be happy. Okay?" Mia said, sounding joyful.

"Okay, Mia, okay. Let's go and do everything. And let's go and be everything. Okay?" Ben said, sounding joyful.

They picked the daisy and hugged and said sorry. They played together and had fun. They fed the ducks and watched the fish. They did not dive in the pond. They were friends and loved each other. They were careful and safe. They were happy and good. They were okay.

name_of_work: The Yachts by William Carlos Williams
content: contend in a sea which the land partly encloses shielding them from the too-heavy blows of an ungoverned ocean which when it chooses tortures the biggest hulls, the best man knows to pit against its beatings, and sinks them pitilessly. Mothlike in mists, scintillant in the minute brilliance of cloudless days, with broad bellying sails they glide to the wind tossing green water from their sharp prows while over them the crew crawls ant-like, solicitously grooming them, releasing, making fast as they turn, lean far over and having caught the wind again, side by side, head for the mark. In a well guarded arena of open water surrounded by lesser and greater craft which, sycophant, lumbering and flittering follow them, they appear youthful, rare as the light of a happy eye, live with the grace of all that in the mind is feckless, free and naturally to be desired. Now the sea which holds them is moody, lapping their glossy sides, as if feeling for some slightest flaw but fails completely. Today no race. Then the wind comes again. The yachts move, jockeying for a start, the signal is set and they are off. Now the waves strike at them but they are too well made, they slip through, though they take in canvas. Arms with hands grasping seek to clutch at the prows. Bodies thrown recklessly in the way are cut aside. It is a sea of faces about them in agony, in despair until the horror of the race dawns staggering the mind; the whole sea become an entanglement of watery bodies lost to the world bearing what they cannot hold. Broken, beaten, desolate, reaching from the dead to be taken up they cry out, failing, failing! their cries rising in waves still as the skillful yachts pass over.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Susie. She was three years old and she lived in a big old house.

One day, Susie wanted to go to school. She knew that she could learn a lot of new and exciting things. She went to school and walked into the classroom.

The classroom was very noisy. Susie looked around and saw a big blackboard on the wall. She thought it was very cool.

But then Susie realised that the blackboard was very dirty. It was full of dirt and dust, and it looked filthy.

Susie didn't know what to do, so she asked her teacher. The teacher told her that they could clean the blackboard together.

So, Susie and her teacher cleaned the blackboard until it was spotless. Now Susie knew that the blackboard was clean and she could learn a lot of new things. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play with his toys and run around outside. One day, Timmy's mommy told him they were going to visit his grandma. Timmy didn't want to go because he wanted to keep playing, but his mommy insisted that they go.

When they got to grandma's house, Timmy smelled something funny. It was smoke coming from the fireplace. Grandma had a fire going to keep the house warm. Timmy thought the smoke looked black and he didn't like it very much.

But then, grandma made Timmy's favorite cookies and he forgot all about the smoke. He had so much fun playing with his grandma and eating cookies that he didn't want to leave when it was time to go home. But his mommy insisted that they had to leave and Timmy said goodbye to his grandma, promising to visit again soon.

Max was a 3 year old who loved to explore. One day, he was walking through a field near his house and he wondered what was beyond it. Then, he saw a big cliff in the distance. He asked his mum what was on the other side.

"I don't know," said his mum. "Let's go and find out."

Max and his mum hopped and skipped to the cliff. Max looked up and wondered how he could get to the top. Suddenly he heard a voice.

"If you can climb to the top I'll give you a prize!" it said.

Max looked down and saw a competitive little boy with a stick. Max smiled and immediately started to climb up the cliff. He stumbled at first but soon he was nearly at the top.

The other boy began to climb too. When Max was getting tired, his mum cheered him on. At last, Max got to the top and the other boy followed shortly after. 

"Well done!" cheered his mum. "You both did great."

Max smiled as his mum gave them both a prize. He was really glad he had been brave enough to climb the cliff and had been able to wonder about what was on the other side.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys all day long. One day, she went to the park to play with her friends. They were running around and having fun. Suddenly, a playful puppy appeared out of nowhere and started chasing them.

Lily and her friends were scared at first, but then they saw how friendly the puppy was. They started to play with him and he became their new friend. They played together for a while, but then it was time for the puppy to go home. 

As the puppy left, the park became quiet again. Lily turned to her friend and said, "I wish the playful puppy could stay and play with us forever." Her friend replied, "Maybe he will come back tomorrow!" And Lily smiled, happy to have made a new friend.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Ben. She was full of joy, and loved to explore the world around her.

One day, Ben was walking in the park when she saw a wallet on the ground. She bent down and grabbed it. 

Just then, a man came rushing up to her. He said: "That's my wallet! I put it down and forgot about it. Thank you so much for being gentle and grabbing it for me!". 

Ben smiled and handed the wallet to the man. She said with a giggle: "You're welcome sir. I'm so glad I found your wallet for you!". 

The man thanked Ben again, and walked away with his wallet. Ben was happy, knowing that she had done a kind act that day.

Once upon a time there was a family that loved to drive. They went on long drives every weekend and always had a lovely time. 

One Saturday, they decided to drive to the mountains. Along the way, the dad stopped at a store to buy some yummy pasta. 

They set up a picnic in the forest and had a lovely time. They enjoyed a picnic lunch of pasta with cheese and vegetables and then hit the road again. Along the way they sang their favorite songs and laughed the whole way. They eventually made it back home, but they all had the most wonderful day. 

The family was so happy that they had a lovely day out and enjoyed pasta together on their drive. They smiled and laughed, knowing that there was nothing better than spending time together doing something they all loved.

name_of_work: In Response to a Rumor That the Oldest Whorehouse in Wheeling, West Virginia Has Been Condemned by James Wright
content: I will grieve alone, As I strolled alone, years ago, down along The Ohio shore. I hid in the hobo jungle weeds Upstream from the sewer main, Pondering, gazing. I saw, down river, At Twenty-third and Water Streets By the vinegar works, The doors open in early evening. Swinging their purses, the women Poured down the long street to the river And into the river. I do not know how it was They could drown every evening. What time near dawn did they climb up the other shore, Drying their wings? For the river at Wheeling, West Virginia, Has only two shores: The one in hell, the other In Bridgeport, Ohio. And nobody would commit suicide, only To find beyond death Bridgeport, Ohio.

name_of_work: Wedding Cake by Naomi Shihab Nye
content: Once on a plane a woman asked me to hold her baby and disappeared. I figured it was safe, our being on a plane and all. How far could she go? She returned one hour later, having changed her clothes and washed her hair. I didn't recognize her. By this time the baby and I had examined each other's necks. We had cried a little. I had a silver bracelet and a watch. Gold studs glittered in the baby's ears. She wore a tiny white dress leafed with layers like a wedding cake. I did not want to give her back. The baby's curls coiled tightly against her scalp, another alphabet. I read new new new. My mother gets tired. I'll chew your hand. The baby left my skirt crumpled, my lap aching. Now I'm her secret guardian, the little nub of dream that rises slightly but won't come clear. As she grows, as she feels ill at ease, I'll bob my knee. What will she forget? Whom will she marry? He'd better check with me. I'll say once she flew dressed like a cake between two doilies of cloud. She could slip the card into a pocket, pull it out. Already she knew the small finger was funnier than the whole arm.

Tom and Jen were brother and sister. They liked to play outside in the big yard. One day, they saw a hole in the ground. It was a pit. They wondered what was inside.

"Let's go and look," Tom said. He was brave and independent. He did not like to ask for help.

"No, Tom, it's too dark and deep," Jen said. She was careful and smart. She did not want to get hurt. "Mom said to stay away from the pit. She said it's dangerous."

"Mom is not here. She went to the store. And I'm not scared. I can do it by myself," Tom said. He did not listen to Jen. He wanted to have fun.

"Please, Tom, don't go. Promise me you won't go," Jen said. She was worried and sad. She loved her brother.

"Okay, okay, I promise. I won't go," Tom said. He lied to Jen. He did not mean it. He waited for Jen to turn around. Then he ran to the pit.

Jen heard a scream. She turned around and saw Tom fall into the pit. She ran to the pit and looked down. She saw Tom lying on the ground. He was hurt and scared. He cried for help.

"Tom, Tom, are you okay?" Jen shouted. She was scared and sorry. She wished she could help.

"Jen, Jen, I'm sorry. I broke my promise. I was stupid. Please help me," Tom shouted. He was sorry and ashamed. He wished he had listened.

Jen ran to the house and called Mom. Mom came home and called the firemen. The firemen came and got Tom out of the pit. They took him to the hospital. He had a broken leg and some scratches. He was lucky.

Mom hugged Jen and Tom. She was angry and relieved. She scolded Tom for being foolish and praised Jen for being brave. She said they should always keep their promises and stay away from the pit.

Tom learned his lesson. He said sorry to Jen and Mom. He said he would never lie again. He said he would be more careful and smart. He said he would listen to Jen and Mom. He said he loved them.

Jen forgave Tom. She said she was glad he was okay. She said she would always help him. She said she loved him.

They hugged and kissed. They were happy and safe. They were brother and sister.

Once there was a brave little girl named Rose. One day, Rose was walking in a dark forest, when suddenly she heard a terrible noise. It scared her, so she stopped walking and looked around.

Then she saw something. It was at the end of the forest. It was pointing at her! Rose was so scared, she started to run away.

But the thing was following her! As Rose ran, it kept getting closer and closer. She started running faster and faster, until she was at the edge of the forest.

When Rose looked back, she saw the thing was gone. She was relieved and breathed a sigh of relief. Rose was so happy that the terrible thing didn't scare her. From then on, she was careful not to walk too far into the forest.

From the window I saw the horses. I was in Berlin, in winter. The light was without light, the sky without sky. The air white like wet bread. And from my window a vacant arena, bitten by the teeth of winter. Suddenly led by a man, ten horses stepped out into the mist. Hardly had they surged forth, like flame, than to my eyes they filled the whole world, empty till then. Perfect, ablaze, they were like ten gods with pure white hoofs, with manes like a dream of salt. Their rumps were worlds and oranges. Their color was honey, amber, fire. Their necks were towers cut from the stone of pride, and behind their transparent eyes energy raged, like a prisoner. And there, in the silence, in the middle of the day, of the dark, slovenly winter, the intense horses were the blood and rhythm, the animating treasure of life. I looked. I looked and was reborn: without knowing it, there, was the fountain, the dance of gold, the sky, the fire that revived in beauty. I have forgotten that dark Berlin winter. I will not forget the light of the horses.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, Lily saw a big hurricane coming towards her house. She was scared and didn't know what to do.

Lily's mom said, "We need to go to the basement to be safe from the hurricane." But Lily was being selfish and didn't want to leave her toys behind. 

Her mom said, "Lily, we need to go now. We can't reach the basement if we wait too long." 

Lily finally understood and grabbed her favorite toy, a teddy bear, and followed her mom to the basement. They waited until the hurricane passed and then went back upstairs to see the damage. Thankfully, their house was okay, but Lily learned that sometimes it's important to think of others and not just herself.

name_of_work: Facts About the Moon by Dorianne Laux
content: The moon is backing away from us an inch and a half each year. That means if you're like me and were born around fifty years ago the moon was a full six feet closer to the earth. What's a person supposed to do? I feel the gray cloud of consternation travel across my face. I begin thinking about the moon-lit past, how if you go back far enough you can imagine the breathtaking hugeness of the moon, prehistoric solar eclipses when the moon covered the sun so completely there was no corona, only a darkness we had no word for. And future eclipses will look like this: the moon a small black pupil in the eye of the sun. But these are bald facts. What bothers me most is that someday the moon will spiral right out of orbit and all land-based life will die. The moon keeps the oceans from swallowing the shores, keeps the electromagnetic fields in check at the polar ends of the earth. And please don't tell me what I already know, that it won't happen for a long time. I don't care. I'm afraid of what will happen to the moon. Forget us. We don't deserve the moon. Maybe we once did but not now after all we've done. These nights I harbor a secret pity for the moon, rolling around alone in space without her milky planet, her only child, a mother who's lost a child, a bad child, a greedy child or maybe a grown boy who's murdered and raped, a mother can't help it, she loves that boy anyway, and in spite of herself she misses him, and if you sit beside her on the padded hospital bench outside the door to his room you can't not take her hand, listen to her while she weeps, telling you how sweet he was, how blue his eyes, and you know she's only romanticizing, that she's conveniently forgotten the bruises and booze, the stolen car, the day he ripped the phones from the walls, and you want to slap her back to sanity, remind her of the truth: he was a leech, a fuckup, a little shit, and you almost do until she lifts her pale puffy face, her eyes two craters and then you can't help it either, you know love when you see it, you can feel its lunar strength, its brutal pull.

You endless torments that my rest oppress, How long will you delight in my sad pain? Will never Love your favour more express? Shall I still live, and ever feel disdain? Alas, now stay, and let my grief obtain Some end; feed not my heart with sharp distress. Let me once see my cruel fortunes gain At least release, and long-felt woes redress. Let not the blame of cruelty disgrace The honoured title of your godhead Love; Give not just cause for me to say a place Is found for rage alone on me to move. O quickly end, and do not long debate My needful aid, lest help do come too late.

name_of_work: The Eagle and the Mole by Elinor Wylie
content: Avoid the reeking herd, Shun the polluted flock, Live like that stoic bird, The eagle of the rock. The huddled warmth of crowds Begets and fosters hate; He keeps above the clouds His cliff inviolate. When flocks are folded warm, And herds to shelter run, He sails above the storm, He stares into the sun. If in the eagle's track Your sinews cannot leap, Avoid the lathered pack, Turn from the steaming sheep. If you would keep your soul From spotted sight or sound, Live like the velvet mole: Go burrow underground. And there hold intercourse With roots of trees and stones, With rivers at their source, And disembodied bones.

Once upon a time, there was a log in a hot forest. The log was all alone, with no one to play with.

One day, a bird flew down and landed on the log. "Hello," said the bird. "Would you like to play with me?"

The log was very happy! It shouted with joy. "Yes, I would love to play with you."

So the bird and the log played together in the hot forest all day. They ran around and laughed. When it was time for the bird to go, the log thanked the bird for being its friend.

The bird smiled. "You are welcome," it said, "I had a great time."

Then, the bird flew away, leaving the log all alone again. But the log knew it would never forget its new friend, and it was so happy.

One day, Carl went outside to play with his friends. But when he got there, he realized that all of them had gone home for the week. Carl sighed sadly and looked around the empty playground. Suddenly, he heard a mysterious voice whispering to him. 

"Follow me," it said. 

Cautiously, Carl followed the voice. He walked until he reached a beautiful meadow. Butterflies fluttered around the vibrant flowers, and Carl smiled in delight. He spotted something glittering in the distance. 

As he walked closer, Carl's eyes widened in amazement: it was a chest filled with treasure! He gasped in surprise and opened the chest.

Suddenly, the mysterious voice spoke again.

"We'll meet again next week," it said.

Startled, Carl looked around but could not spot anyone. He puzzled over the mysterious voice, but eventually realized he would have to wait until next week to find out who it belonged to. Excitement bubbled inside of him as he left, thinking of the mystery ahead.

Anna and Ben like to play with their toys on the carpet. They have cars, dolls, blocks and books. They share their toys and have fun. But sometimes they want the same toy and they fight.

One day, Anna and Ben both want the red car. It is their favorite car. It can go fast and make noises. Anna says, "I want the red car. It is mine." Ben says, "No, I want the red car. It is mine." They pull the car from each other and yell.

Mom hears them and comes to the room. She is angry. She says, "Stop fighting. You have to share your toys. If you can't share, you can't play." She takes the red car and puts it on the shelf. She says, "No one can play with the red car until you say sorry and hug."

Anna and Ben are sad. They don't want to lose the red car. They look at each other and feel sorry. They say, "Sorry, Anna." "Sorry, Ben." They hug and smile. Mom sees them and smiles too. She says, "That's better. Now you can play nicely." She gives them the red car and a kiss.

Anna and Ben are happy. They play with the red car and their other toys. They take turns and help each other. They say, "Thank you, Mom." "You're welcome, Anna and Ben." They have fun on the carpet.

Once upon a time there was a yellow parade. The parade was full of happy people and animals all wearing yellow. 

It was getting dark when the parade vanished. Poof! Just like that it was gone. Everyone was so confused- one minute there was a parade and the next it was gone!

The next day, they searched everywhere for the yellow parade. It was nowhere to be found. Had it really gone, or was it hiding somewhere? 

Just when they were about to give up, the yellow parade was seen down the street. The parade had reappeared! Everyone cheered and waved as the parade passed. Now they will never forget the yellow parade!

And this from the second or third millennium B.C., a female, aged about twenty-two. A white, fine skull, full up with darkness As a shell with sea, drowned in the centuries. Small, perfect. The cranium would fit the palm Of a man's hand. Some plague or violence Destroyed her, and her whiteness lay safe in a shroud Of silence, undisturbed, unrained on, dark For four thousand years. Till a tractor in summer Biting its way through the longcairn for supplies Of stone, broke open the grave and let a crowd of light Stare in at her, and she stared quietly back. . As I look at her I feel none of the shock The farmer felt as, unprepared, he found her. Here in the museum, like death in hospital, Reasons are given, labels, causes, catalogues. The smell of death is done. Left, only her bone Purity, the light and shade beauty that her man Was denied sight of, the perfect edge of the place Where the pieces join, with no mistakes, like boundaries. She's a tree in winter, stripped white on a black sky, Leafless formality, brow, bough in fine relief. I, at some other season, illustrate the tree Fleshed, with woman's hair and colours and the rustling Blood, the troubled mind that she has overthrown. We stare at each other, dark into sightless Dark, seeing only ourselves in the black pools, Gulping the risen sea that booms in the shell.

name_of_work: In and Out of Time by Maya Angelou
content: The sun has come. The mist has gone. We see in the distance... our long way home. I was always yours to have. You were always mine. We have loved each other in and out of time. When the first stone looked up at the blazing sun and the first tree struggled up from the forest floor I had always loved you more. You freed your braids... gave your hair to the breeze. It hummed like a hive of honey bees. I reached in the mass for the sweet honey comb there... Mmmm... God how I love your hair. You saw me bludgeoned by circumstance. Lost, injured, hurt by chance. I screamed to the heavens... loudly screamed... Trying to change our nightmares into dreams... The sun has come. The mist has gone. We see in the distance our long way home. I was always yours to have. You were always mine. We have loved each other in and out in and out in and out of time.

One day, there was a restless boot. He jogged all around the house, looking for something to do. He jogged from the kitchen, to the bedroom, and then to the living room. But he still wasn't happy. 

So he jogged outside to find something exciting. He saw a big tree and decided to explore. He jogged around the tree, looking up and all around. Then he jogged to the pond and saw some ducks. He watched the ducks swim around, but he wanted to swim too. 

The boot jogged back to the house and put the biggest bucket he could find onto his head. Then, he jogged down to the pond and jumped right in. He swam around, feeling so much better now that he was in the water. 

Finally, the boot was happy. He jogged back to the house and took a long, peaceful nap. From then on, the boot wasn't restless anymore. He knew just how to have fun.

Tom and Lily were playing in the park. They liked to run and jump and slide. They saw a big box near the trees. It had a picture of a lion on it.

"Let's see what's inside!" Tom said. He ran to the box and tried to open it. He used his hands to tear the tape and the paper.

Lily followed him. She was curious too. She helped him tear the box. They made a lot of noise.

Suddenly, they heard a roar. It was loud and scary. They looked inside the box and saw a real lion. It was smelly and angry. It had sharp teeth and claws.

Tom and Lily screamed. They dropped the box and ran away. They did not want to play with the lion. They wanted to go home.

The lion jumped out of the box. It was hungry and tired. It had been in the box for a long time. It did not like the park. It wanted to go back to the zoo.

It saw Tom and Lily running. It chased them. It wanted to catch them and eat them.

But then, it saw a man in a uniform. He had a big truck and a net. He was from the zoo. He had been looking for the lion. He had lost it when he was moving it to a new cage.

He threw the net over the lion. He put it back in the truck. He drove away.

Tom and Lily stopped running. They were safe. They hugged each other. They were glad the man took the lion away. They learned a lesson. They would never tear a box with a lion on it again.

Once upon a time there was a young boy named Sam. He saw his daddy using a razor to shave his face every morning. Sam asked his daddy what the razor was for. Daddy explained, "A razor is a special tool used to trim and shape your beard. It is very important to keep a neat and tidy face."

Sam was curious and asked, "Can I use it too?" The father smiled and said, "It is not safe for you to use a razor, son. It's a grown-up tool."

But Sam didn't understand. He kept asking why he couldn't use it, so his father decided to explain in a different way. He said, "A razor is like a toy. It can be fun to play with, but it can also be dangerous if it is not used correctly. So I need you to understand that it is important for only adults to use it."

Sam finally understood, and he thanked his father for explaining it to him. From then on, Sam always remembered not to touch a razor and only let grown-ups use it.

name_of_work: When All My Five and Country Senses See by Dylan Thomas
content: When all my five and country senses see, The fingers will forget green thumbs and mark How, through the halfmoon's vegetable eye, Husk of young stars and handfull zodiac, Love in the frost is pared and wintered by, The whispering ears will watch love drummed away Down breeze and shell to a discordant beach, And, lashed to syllables, the lynx tongue cry That her fond wounds are mended bitterly. My nostrils see her breath burn like a bush. My one and noble heart has witnesses In all love's countries, that will grope awake; And when blind sleep drops on the spying senses, The heart is sensual, though five eyes break.

Jen and Tom were twins who liked to travel with their mom and dad. They went to many places and saw many things. One day, they went to a farm where they could pick blueberries. Jen and Tom loved blueberries. They were sweet and juicy and made their tongues blue.

"Look, mom, look, dad, we found so many blueberries!" Jen and Tom said, showing their baskets full of berries.

"Good job, kids, you can eat some now and we'll take the rest home," mom and dad said, smiling.

Jen and Tom ate some blueberries and felt happy. They wanted to eat more, but mom and dad said they had to save some for later. Jen and Tom did not like that. They wanted to eat all the blueberries now. They were upset.

When mom and dad were not looking, Jen and Tom sneaked back to the blueberry bushes. They ate more and more blueberries, until their baskets were empty. They did not care that they were being greedy. They just wanted more blueberries.

But then, something bad happened. Jen and Tom felt sick. Their tummies hurt and they felt like throwing up. They ran to mom and dad and cried.

"Mom, dad, we don't feel good, we ate too many blueberries," Jen and Tom said, feeling sorry.

Mom and dad were angry and worried. They scolded Jen and Tom for being naughty and not listening. They took them to the car and drove to the doctor. The doctor gave them some medicine and told them to rest. Jen and Tom had to stay in bed for a long time. They missed their next travel and they could not eat blueberries for a while. They learned their lesson and never ate too many blueberries again.

Ben and Lily liked to play with their toy cars. They had many cars of different colors and sizes. They liked to make noises and race them on the floor. One day, they found a big car that had a battery inside. It could move by itself when they pushed a button.

"Wow, this car is mighty!" Ben said. "It is faster and louder than the others. Let's play with it outside!"

"Okay!" Lily said. They took the car and ran to the backyard. They found a spot of dirt and put the car on it. They pushed the button and watched the car zoom around.

"Vroom, vroom!" they shouted. They had fun chasing the car and making it turn and spin. They played until the sun was low in the sky.

"Ben, Lily, time to come in!" their mom called. "It's getting dark and dinner is ready!"

"Okay, mom!" they said. They ran to the car and picked it up. But the car did not move or make noise anymore. The battery was dead.

"Oh no, the car is broken!" Ben said. "What can we do?"

"I have an idea!" Lily said. "Let's bury the car in the dirt. Maybe it will grow a new battery!"

"Really?" Ben said. "Will that work?"

"Sure!" Lily said. "Everything grows in the dirt. Flowers, trees, carrots. Why not batteries?"

"Okay, let's try it!" Ben said. They dug a hole in the dirt and put the car in it. They covered it with more dirt and patted it down.

"There, the car is buried!" Lily said. "Now we have to wait and see what happens!"

They ran inside and ate their dinner. They forgot about the car and played with their other toys. The next day, they remembered the car and ran outside to dig it up. They hoped to see a new battery or maybe even a bigger car.

But when they reached the spot of dirt, they saw nothing. The car was gone. Someone had taken it.

"Hey, where is our car?" Ben said. "Who took it?"

"I don't know!" Lily said. "Maybe a dog or a bird or a monster!"

They looked around and saw no sign of their car. They felt sad and angry. They had lost their mighty car. They wished they had not buried it. They wished they had taken it inside and asked their mom for a new battery.

They learned a hard lesson. Burying things in the dirt does not make them grow. It only makes them disappear.

Tim and Sue like to play in the park. They like to swing, slide and run. One day, they see a big pie on a table. The pie smells good and looks yummy.

"Who made this pie?" Tim asks.

"I don't know. Maybe someone left it here for us," Sue says.

They go to the table and look at the pie. It has red and blue berries on top. They want to taste it.

"Can we have some pie?" Tim asks.

"Let's wait a bit. Maybe the person who made it will come back," Sue says.

They sit on the bench and watch the pie. They see a bird fly to the pie. The bird pecks at the berries. They see a cat jump on the table. The cat licks the crust. They see a dog run to the pie. The dog bites a big piece.

"Hey, stop! That's our pie!" Tim and Sue shout.

They run to the table and try to save the pie. But it is too late. The pie is gone. Only some crumbs remain.

Tim and Sue are sad. They wanted to eat the pie. They look at the bird, the cat and the dog. They are happy. They have full bellies.

"That's not fair. They took our pie," Tim says.

"They are funny. They like pie too," Sue says.

They laugh. They are not sad anymore. They go back to play in the park. They have fun. They forget about the pie.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy. He was brave and kind. Every day, he went for a walk in his favorite park.

One day, he noticed a lady sitting on a bench in the park. She looked so sad, he felt like he had to talk to her. He bravely walked up to her and said hello. 

The lady was surprised. She stopped crying and smiled at the little boy. She asked him why he had come to talk to her. 

He replied, "I wanted to know why you were so sad".

The lady smiled and told the little boy that she was feeling overwhelmed with her job. She said that it was very hard to be persistent every day. 

The little boy nodded and said, "Maybe you just need to take a break". The lady smiled and said that was a great idea. 

The next day, when the little boy came to the park, the lady was smiling. She waved and said, "Thank you for helping me yesterday. I feel much better now". 

The little boy was so happy, he smiled and skipped all the way home.

name_of_work: To the Moon by Percy Bysshe Shelley
content: I Art thou pale for weariness Of climbing heaven and gazing on the earth, Wandering companionless Among the stars that have a different birth, -- And ever changing, like a joyless eye That finds no object worth its constancy? II Thou chosen sister of the Spirit, That gazes on thee till in thee it pities ...

Once upon a time, there was a man who had a big farm. He had many animals, like cows, pigs, and chickens. One day, he decided to sell some of his cows. He went to the market and found a buyer who wanted to buy his cows. The man was happy because he could earn some money.

After he sold the cows, he went back to his farm. He noticed that it was very quiet there. He looked around and saw that all the animals were hidden behind the barn. They were scared because they thought the man was going to sell them too. But the man told them that he loved them and would never sell them. The animals felt happy and came out of hiding.

One day, a little boy and his mom were walking through the countryside. They came to a big, deep well. He stopped and asked his mom, "What is this?" She replied, "It's a well. It's very deep." The little boy peered in to the well and said, "I think I hear something!" His mom leaned in to listen, but she couldn't hear anything. "I think it's a person inside the well," said the little boy. 

Suddenly, a voice from down in the well said "Help me, I'm stuck!" The little boy and his mom were so surprised. The voice cried out, "Please help me! I can't get out!". The little boy's mom put her hand over his ear and said, "It's okay, we'll help."

The mom started to weep, as she realized the person in the well was deaf. She looked around and found some rope, so she lowered it down to the person. Eventually he was able to climb out of the well. 

The little boy hugged the man and said, "Don't worry, you're safe now". The man smiled and nodded in agreement. The little boy and his mom walked away with a feeling of joy, knowing that they had saved the day.

name_of_work: In the Desert by Stephen Crane
content: In the desert I saw a creature, naked, bestial, Who, squatting upon the ground, Held his heart in his hands, And ate of it. I said, "Is it good, friend?" "It is bitter--bitter," he answered; "But I like it "Because it is bitter, "And because it is my heart."

Once upon a time, there was a little boy called Joe. Joe lived in a small village near a mountain. It was summer and the weather was beautiful. 

One day, Joe decided to go on an adventure. He went to the top of the mountain and saw a big lake. He filled up a cup with water and decided to carry it home.

On his way back, Joe encountered a strong wind. The wind blew the water out of the cup and it was pouring all over the ground. Joe was sad - he wanted to bring the water back for his family, but it was impossible.

Then, Joe's father came up to him and said, "Joe, when life gives you difficult moments, remember to stay strong. Life is full of weather, but you should keep your head up. And no matter what, try to do your best."

The moral of Joe's story is that life won't always be easy, but if you stay strong, no matter the weather, you will be able to overcome whatever comes your way and make the best of it.

Anna and Ben are twins. They like to play with cards. They have many cards with animals and colors. They make piles and match them.

One day, Mom says, "We need to go to the store. Do you want to come with me?"

Anna and Ben say, "Yes, yes, we want to go!"

They put on their shoes and coats. They take their cards with them. They want to show them to the people at the store.

Mom drives the car to the store. She is fast. Anna and Ben look out the window. They see trees and houses and cars. They say, "Look, look, a red car! Look, look, a big dog!"

They get to the store. Mom says, "Stay with me, please. Do not run away."

Anna and Ben say, "OK, Mom. We will stay with you."

They go inside the store. They see many things. They see food and clothes and toys. They see people and carts and shelves.

Anna and Ben see a lady with a card. The card has a picture of a flower. Anna and Ben like flowers. They go to the lady and say, "Hello, hello, we have cards too! Look, look, a lion! Look, look, a blue!"

The lady smiles. She says, "Hello, hello, you have nice cards. You are very smart. Can I see your cards?"

Anna and Ben show their cards to the lady. They are happy. They talk to the lady. They tell her the names of the animals and the colors.

Mom sees Anna and Ben. She says, "There you are! I was looking for you. Who is your friend?"

Anna and Ben say, "This is the lady with the flower card. She is nice. She likes our cards."

Mom says, "Hello, lady with the flower card. I am sorry if my twins bothered you. They are very curious."

The lady says, "No, no, they did not bother me. They are very sweet. They have good manners."

Mom says, "Thank you, thank you. You are very kind. Come on, Anna and Ben. We need to go. We have to buy some things."

Anna and Ben say, "Bye, bye, lady with the flower card. Thank you for talking to us. We hope to see you again."

The lady says, "Bye, bye, Anna and Ben. Thank you for showing me your cards. I hope to see you again too."

Anna and Ben take their cards and follow Mom. They go to the checkout. They see a man with a machine. The machine makes a beep sound. The man scans the things that Mom buys. He is slow. Anna and Ben are bored. They play with their cards. They make piles and match them. They wait for Mom to finish.

Mom pays the man. She says, "Thank you, thank you. Have a nice day."

The man says, "You're welcome, you're welcome. Have a nice day too."

Mom takes the bags. She says, "Let's go, Anna and Ben. We are done."

Anna and Ben say, "OK, Mom. We are done too."

They go to the car. They put their cards and the bags in the car. They get in the car. Mom drives the car home. She is fast. Anna and Ben look out the window. They see trees and houses and cars. They say, "Look, look, a yellow car! Look, look, a small cat!"

They get home. They take their cards and the bags inside. They say, "We had fun at the store. We met a lady with a flower card. She was nice. She liked our cards."

Mom says, "I'm glad you had fun. You were good at the store. You can play with your cards now. But first, help me put away the things we bought."

Anna and Ben say, "OK, Mom. We will help you. Then we will play with our cards."

They help Mom put away the things. Then they play with their cards. They make piles and match them. They are happy. They love their cards. They love Mom. They love each other. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a lazy cat named Whiskers. Whiskers liked to sleep all day and didn't like to play with his toys. One day, Whiskers saw a butterfly outside and decided to catch it. He ran outside and chased the butterfly, but it flew away.

Whiskers then saw a net on the ground and decided to use it to catch the butterfly. He picked up the net and tried to catch the butterfly, but it was too fast. Whiskers was sad that he couldn't catch the butterfly.

Later that day, Whiskers saw his owner display some new toys for him to play with. Whiskers was excited and forgot all about the butterfly. He played with his new toys and was very happy. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a shiny gold necklace that she loved to wear every day. One day, she lost her necklace while playing in the park. She was very sad and didn't know what to do.

Her friend, Timmy, saw that she was sad and asked her what was wrong. Lily told him that she lost her gold necklace and couldn't find it. Timmy said, "Don't be sad, I will help you find it. Where did you last have it?"

Lily answered, "I had it on when I was playing on the swings." So, they went back to the swings and searched for the necklace. After a few minutes, Timmy found it lying in the grass. Lily was so happy and thanked Timmy for helping her. They both went home with big smiles on their faces.

Lila and Tom were playing in the kitchen. They wanted to make a cake for their mom. They saw a big bag of sugar on the shelf. They tried to reach it, but it was too high.

"Let's stretch our arms," Tom said. "Maybe we can get it."

They stretched and stretched, but they still could not touch the sugar. They saw a chair near the table. They had an idea.

"Let's use the chair," Lila said. "We can climb on it and get the sugar."

They dragged the chair to the shelf. They took turns to climb on it. Tom went first. He grabbed the sugar and threw it to Lila. Lila caught it and put it on the table. Then she climbed on the chair and looked for more things to make the cake.

She saw a bottle of milk, a jar of honey, and a box of eggs. She threw them to Tom one by one. Tom caught them and put them on the table. They were happy. They had everything they needed to make the cake.

But they did not see their dad coming into the kitchen. He saw the mess they made. He saw the sugar, the milk, the honey, and the eggs on the table. He saw the chair near the shelf. He saw Lila and Tom smiling.

He was not happy. He was angry. He had a harsh voice.

"What are you doing?" he asked. "You are not supposed to play with the food. You are making a big mess. You are wasting the sugar. You are in trouble."

Lila and Tom were scared. They did not want to make their dad angry. They did not want to be in trouble. They did not want to make the cake anymore.

They said sorry to their dad. They said they wanted to make a cake for their mom. They said they did not know it was bad to play with the food.

Their dad sighed. He saw they were sorry. He saw they wanted to do something nice for their mom. He softened his voice.

"I know you wanted to make a cake for your mom," he said. "But you have to ask me or mom before you use the food. You have to be careful and clean. You have to follow the recipe. You can't just throw things around. Do you understand?"

Lila and Tom nodded. They understood. They said sorry again. They said they would help their dad clean the mess. They said they would learn how to make a cake the right way.

Their dad smiled. He hugged them. He said he loved them. He said he would help them make a cake for their mom. He said they would use less sugar. He said they would have fun. He said they would make their mom happy.

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Abigail. She was three years old. One day, Abigail was out in the garden with her mom. Abigail saw a celery plant growing in the garden and asked her mom what it was. 

"That's celery, sweetie," said her mom. 

"What's it for?" asked Abigail.

"You can eat it," replied her mom.

Abigail was excited. She called out to her dad. "Daddy! Daddy! Look what I found! Celery!"

Abigail's dad came to the garden to see her. He picked a celery stalk and tasted it. "Mmm, it's good!" he said.

But he could tell the celery was spoiled. It was a little bit brown in the middle. 

Abigail's dad smiled at her. "Time to go inside, Abigail. Let's get some fresh celery from the store instead."

Once upon a time there was a small girl named Jane. Jane was very smart and wanted to succeed in a race. She had heard of the race from her big sister who said she wanted to enter it too.

So one day, Jane got ready with her pink shoes on and set off to join the race. When she arrived, she saw lots of other people all wearing different coloured clothes.

At the start of the race, Jane was a bit scared but she took a deep breath and ran forward. All of a sudden, she felt fast and strong and she ran past the other people. She flew across the finish line and she had won!

Jane was so happy - she had succeeded in the race. Everyone cheered for her and said she was really smart. Jane was the happiest she had ever been and ran to hug her big sister.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a big, blue tent. She was very proud of her tent. Lily loved to play in her tent with her toys.

One day, it started to rain. Lily wanted to protect her toys from getting wet. So, she took them all into her tent. She put her teddy bear, her doll, and her toy car inside the tent. They were all safe from the rain.

Lily felt happy and proud that she could protect her toys. She knew that her tent was a special place. And now, her toys were safe and dry. They could play together again when the rain stopped.

Now the leaves are falling fast, Nurse's flowers will not last; Nurses to the graves are gone, And the prams go rolling on. Whispering neighbours, left and right, Pluck us from the real delight; And the active hands must freeze Lonely on the separate knees. Dead in hundreds at the back Follow wooden in our track, Arms raised stiffly to reprove In false attitudes of love. Starving through the leafless wood Trolls run scolding for their food; And the nightingale is dumb, And the angel will not come. Cold, impossible, ahead Lifts the mountain's lovely head Whose white waterfall could bless Travellers in their last distress.

John was a young boy who loved to tell jokes. Every day he would go out, looking for new jokes to tell his friends. He loved the laughter it brought him and his friends.

One day, John decided to go farther than he ever had before. He set off, feeling excited and a little bit dizzy at the same time.

The farther he went, the more wild and strange things he found. He thought he saw a giant growing in the distance. But he laughed it off, thinking it was just a tall tree.

But as he kept walking, the giant started to get bigger and bigger. John realized too late that it wasnâ€™t a joke. He had stumbled into danger.

The giant was getting closer, it was headed his way. John tried to run away but he was too weak and dizzy. The giant caught up and John was never seen again.

name_of_work: Hunters in the Snow by William Carlos Williams
content: The over-all picture is winter icy mountains in the background the return from the hunt it is toward evening from the left sturdy hunters lead in their pack the inn-sign hanging from a broken hinge is a stag a crucifix between his antlers the cold inn yard is deserted but for a huge bonfire that flares wind-driven tended by women who cluster about it to the right beyond the hill is a pattern of skaters Brueghel the painter concerned with it all has chosen a winter-struck bush for his foreground to complete the picture

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to read books every day. One day, he found a big book with lots of words he didn't know. It was called a dictionary. Timmy asked his mom what it was for, and she said it helps you learn new words.

Timmy was excited to use the dictionary, but his mom warned him to be careful. She said the book was heavy and dangerous if it fell on his foot. So, Timmy put the dictionary on a shelf to store it safely. 

Whenever Timmy wanted to learn a new word, he would take the dictionary down from the shelf and look it up. He was happy to learn new words and use them in his sentences. And he always remembered to put the dictionary back on the shelf when he was done, so it would stay safe and not be dangerous. The end.

In a dream I spoke with the Cyprus-born, And said to her, "Mother of beauty, mother of joy, Why hast thou given to men "This thing called love, like the ache of a wound In beauty's side, To burn and throb and be quelled for an hour And never wholly depart?" And the daughter of Cyprus said to me, "Child of the earth, Behold, all things are born and attain, But only as they desire,-- "The sun that is strong, the gods that are wise, The loving heart, Deeds and knowledge and beauty and joy,-- But before all else was desire."

Once upon a time there was a big house. Everyone who lived inside the house was always happy and healthy. But there was one thing they all hated.

Every morning they had to clean the house. They had to wash the dishes, sweep the floors, and tidy up all the toys. The kids didn't want to spend all their time cleaning, so they tried to find a way out.

One day, the kids found a mouse. The mouse was very happy and friendly. "I can help you clean the house," said the mouse. The kids were so excited they quickly agreed.

From then on, every morning the mouse helped the kids clean the house. The kids no longer had to do all the hard work. They were so happy and grateful for their new friend. 

Now, everyone in the house loved their helpful mouse and no longer hated cleaning the house.

name_of_work: "Let the world's sharpness..." Sonnets from the Portuguese (XXIV) by Elizabeth Barrett Browning
content: Let the world's sharpness, like a clasping knife, Shut in upon itself and do no harm In this close hand of Love, now soft and warm, And let us hear no sound of human strife After the click of the shutting. Life to life-- I lean upon thee, Dear, without alarm, And feel as safe as guarded by a charm Against the stab of worldlings, who if rife Are weak to injure. Very whitely still The lilies of our lives may reassure Their blossoms from their roots, accessible Alone to heavenly dews that drop not fewer, Growing straight, out of man's reach, on the hill. God only, who made us rich, can make us poor.

Lily and Ben like to play with their toy trains. They have many trains of different colors and sizes. They make tracks on the floor and pretend to be drivers.

One day, Lily notices a new train in the toy box. It is red and shiny, and has a big engine. She picks it up and shows it to Ben.

"Look, Ben, a new train!" she says. "It is different from our trains. It has a big engine. Can I play with it?"

Ben looks at the new train and nods. He likes the new train too. He thinks it is fast and strong.

"Okay, Lily, you can play with it," he says. "But can I try it later?"

Lily smiles and says yes. She puts the new train on the track and pushes it gently. The train makes a loud noise and moves quickly. Lily and Ben laugh and clap.

The new train is fun to play with. Lily and Ben take turns to drive it. They have a good time with their toy trains.

name_of_work: Part III: The Rime of The Ancient Mariner by S.T. Coleridge
content: There passed a weary time. Each throat Was parched, and glazed each eye. A weary time! a weary time! How glazed each weary eye, When looking westward, I beheld A something in the sky. At first it seemed a little speck, And then it seemed a mist; It moved and moved, and took at last A certain shape, I wist. A speck, a mist, a shape, I wist! And still it neared and neared: As if it dodged a water-sprite, It plunged and tacked and veered. With throats unslaked, with black lips baked, We could nor laugh nor wail; Through utter drought all dumb we stood! I bit my arm, I sucked the blood, And cried, A sail! a sail! With throats unslaked, with black lips baked, Agape they heard me call: Gramercy! they for joy did grin, And all at once their breath drew in. As they were drinking all. See! see! (I cried) she tacks no more! Hither to work us weal; Without a breeze, without a tide, She steadies with upright keel! The western wave was all a-flame. The day was well nigh done! Almost upon the western wave Rested the broad bright Sun; When that strange shape drove suddenly Betwixt us and the Sun. And straight the Sun was flecked with bars, (Heaven's Mother send us grace!) As if through a dungeon-grate he peered With broad and burning face. Alas! (thought I, and my heart beat loud) How fast she nears and nears! Are those her sails that glance in the Sun, Like restless gossameres? Are those her ribs through which the Sun Did peer, as through a grate? And is that Woman all her crew? Is that a DEATH? and are there two? Is DEATH that woman's mate? Her lips were red, her looks were free, Her locks were yellow as gold: Her skin was as white as leprosy, The Night-mare LIFE-IN-DEATH was she, Who thicks man's blood with cold. The naked hulk alongside came, And the twain were casting dice; 'The game is done! I've won! I've won!' Quoth she, and whistles thrice. The Sun's rim dips; the stars rush out; At one stride comes the dark; With far-heard whisper, o'er the sea, Off shot the spectre-bark. We listened and looked sideways up! Fear at my heart, as at a cup, My life-blood seemed to sip! The stars were dim, and thick the night, The steersman's face by his lamp gleamed white; From the sails the dew did drip-- Till clomb above the eastern bar The horned Moon, with one bright star Within the nether tip. One after one, by the star-dogged Moon, Too quick for groan or sigh, Each turned his face with a ghastly pang, And cursed me with his eye. Four times fifty living men, (And I heard nor sigh nor groan) With heavy thump, a lifeless lump, They dropped down one by one. The souls did from their bodies fly,-- They fled to bliss or woe! And every soul, it passed me by, Like the whizz of my cross-bow!

Once upon a time, in a big pond, there was a colorful crocodile. He was very nice and loved to make new friends. One day, he saw a little bird sitting by the pond. The crocodile swam over to say hello.

"Hi, little bird! I am a colorful crocodile. Welcome to my pond," said the crocodile with a big smile. The little bird looked at the crocodile and said, "Hello, colorful crocodile! I am a little bird. Thank you for welcoming me to your pond."

The colorful crocodile and the little bird became good friends. They played in the pond every day. One day, they saw dark clouds in the sky. The colorful crocodile said, "Little bird, I think it will rain soon. Let's find a safe place to hide."

The little bird and the colorful crocodile found a big tree to hide under. They stayed dry and safe from the rain. When the rain stopped, they went back to playing in the pond. The little bird was happy to have a friend like the colorful crocodile, who knew how to keep them both safe and happy.

Once upon a time, there was a mighty penguin named Pete. Pete loved to swim and play with his penguin friends. One day, he wanted to go on an adventure to explore the big, wide world outside of his home.

Pete's mom said, "I permit you to go, but be careful and come back before the sun sets."

Excitedly, Pete waddled away from his family and into the unknown. He met a friendly seal who asked, "Where are you going, little penguin?"

"I'm going on an adventure to see what's out there," replied Pete.

The seal smiled and said, "That sounds like fun! Can I come with you?"

Pete happily agreed and together they explored the vast ocean. They saw colorful fish, big whales, and even a sunken ship. As the sun began to set, Pete realized it was time to head back home.

Returning to his family, Pete exclaimed, "I had the best adventure ever! And I made a new friend too!"

His mom smiled and said, "I'm glad you had fun, my mighty little penguin."

name_of_work: To William Wordsworth by Samuel Taylor Coleridge
content: Friend of the Wise ! and Teacher of the Good ! Into my heart have I received that Lay More than historic, that prophetic Lay Wherein (high theme by thee first sung aright) Of the foundations and the building up Of a Human Spirit thou hast dared to tell What may be told, to the understanding mind Revealable ; and what within the mind By vital breathings secret as the soul Of vernal growth, oft quickens in the heart Thoughts all too deep for words !-- Theme hard as high ! Of smiles spontaneous, and mysterious fears (The first-born they of Reason and twin-birth), Of tides obedient to external force, And currents self-determined, as might seem, Or by some inner Power ; of moments awful, Now in thy inner life, and now abroad, When power streamed from thee, and thy soul received The light reflected, as a light bestowed-- Of fancies fair, and milder hours of youth, Hyblean murmurs of poetic thought Industrious in its joy, in vales and glens Native or outland, lakes and famous hills ! Or on the lonely high-road, when the stars Were rising ; or by secret mountain-streams, The guides and the companions of thy way ! Of more than Fancy, of the Social Sense Distending wide, and man beloved as man, Where France in all her towns lay vibrating Like some becalmed bark beneath the burst Of Heaven's immediate thunder, when no cloud Is visible, or shadow on the main. For thou wert there, thine own brows garlanded, Amid the tremor of a realm aglow, Amid the mighty nation jubilant, When from the general heart of human kind Hope sprang forth like a full-born Diety ! --Of that dear Hope afflicted and struck down, So summoned homeward, thenceforth calm and sure From the dread watch-tower of man's absolute self, With light unwaning on her eyes, to look Far on--herself a glory to behold, The Angel of the vision ! Then (last strain) Of Duty, chosen Laws controlling choice, Action and Joy !--An Orphic song indeed, A song divine of high and passionate thoughts To their own music chaunted ! O great Bard ! Ere yet that last strain dying awed the air, With stedfast eye I viewed thee in the choir Of ever-enduring men. The truly great Have all one age, and from one visible space Shed influence ! They, both in power and act, Are permanent, and Time is not with them, Save as it worketh for them, they in it. Nor less a sacred Roll, than those of old, And to be placed, as they, with gradual fame Among the archives of mankind, thy work Makes audible a linked lay of Truth, Of Truth profound a sweet continuous lay, Not learnt, but native, her own natural notes ! Ah ! as I listened with a heart forlorn, The pulses of my being beat anew : And even as Life returns upon the drowned, Life's joy rekindling roused a throng of pains-- Keen pangs of Love, awakening as a babe Turbulent, with an outcry in the heart ; And Fears self-willed, that shunned the eye of Hope ; And Hope that scarce would know itself from Fear ; Sense of past Youth, and Manhood come in vain, And Genius given, and Knowledge won in vain ; And all which I had culled in wood-walks wild, And all which patient toil had reared, and all, Commune with thee had opened out--but flowers Strewed on my corse, and borne upon my bier, In the same coffin, for the self-same grave ! That way no more ! and ill beseems it me, Who came a welcomer in herald's guise, Singing of Glory, and Futurity, To wander back on such unhealthful road, Plucking the poisons of self-harm ! And ill Such intertwine beseems triumphal wreaths Strew'd before thy advancing ! Nor do thou, Sage Bard ! impair the memory of that hour Of thy communion with my nobler mind By pity or grief, already felt too long ! Nor let my words import more blame than needs. The tumult rose and ceased : for Peace is nigh Where Wisdom's voice has found a listening heart. Amid the howl of more than wintry storms, The Halcyon hears the voice of vernal hours Already on the wing. Eve following eve, Dear tranquil time, when the sweet sense of Home Is sweetest ! moments for their own sake hailed And more desired, more precious, for thy song, In silence listening, like a devout child, My soul lay passive, by thy various strain Driven as in surges now beneath the stars, With momentary stars of my own birth, Fair constellated foam, still darting off Into the darkness ; now a tranquil sea, Outspread and bright, yet swelling to the moon. And when--O Friend ! my comforter and guide ! Strong in thyself, and powerful to give strength !-- Thy long sustained Song finally closed, And thy deep voice had ceased--yet thou thyself Wert still before my eyes, and round us both That happy vision of beloved faces-- Scarce conscious, and yet conscious of its close I sate, my being blended in one thought (Thought was it ? or aspiration ? or resolve ?) Absorbed, yet hanging still upon the sound-- And when I rose, I found myself in prayer.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play at the beach with his mommy and daddy. One day, Timmy and his parents went to the ocean. They saw the big waves and the seagulls flying in the sky.

Timmy wanted to play in the water, but he was scared of the big waves. His mommy said, "Don't be embarrassed, Timmy. We can play in the shallow water." Timmy felt happy and ran to the water.

Suddenly, a big wave came and slapped Timmy in the face. He started to cry and said, "I don't want to play in the ocean anymore." His daddy said, "It's okay, Timmy. We can build sandcastles instead." Timmy smiled and they had fun building sandcastles together.

Suddenly,baby came in. He saw the vegetables and shouted "Yum!"

Once there was a frog named Fred. He lived with his family in a pond near a busy road.

On this particular day, Fred was in an argument with his brother. They started to quarrel.

"I don't like it when you take things without asking," Fred said crossly.

"But I think it's fun!" His brother replied.

The traffic on the busy road seemed to grow louder. All of a sudden, Fred had an idea. He asked his brother to come with him.

"I know a place that is unique," explained Fred. "It's a secret pond near the highway, and no one can hear us quarrel there!"

So Fred and his brother hopped down the road, away from all the traffic. They soon came to a small pond with lily pads and a fountain in the middle.

The two frogs played and splashed in the secret pond until they had worked out their quarrel. They were friends again and were glad that Fred had found such a special, unique place.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl who loved to play on her amazing slide. Every day, she would run outside and fly down it over and over again.

The little girl had an incredible idea. She asked her dad if he could lend her a broom. When her dad asked why, she smiled and replied that she wanted to fly even faster down the slide. Her dad thought it was a great idea and gave her the broom. 

The little girl ran back outside and put the broom between her legs. She then went to the top of the slide and pushed off. The little girl was going faster than ever before! 

The little girl's dad could not believe his eyes. The broom allowed her to go down the slide at an incredible speed. He watched as his little girl laughed and cheered with glee.

The little girl was so happy. She was grateful to her dad for lending her the broom as it made playing on the slide extra special. She was so proud of her incredible discovery.

Tom and Amy are friends. They like to play with blocks. They have many blocks of different shapes and colors. They can make houses, cars, towers and more.

One day, they find a new block. It is a light square. It is very shiny and pretty. Tom and Amy both want the light square. They start to fight over it. They pull and push and shout. They are not nice to each other.

The light square falls to the floor. It breaks into many pieces. Tom and Amy are sad. They look at the broken block. They feel sorry. They say sorry to each other. They hug and make up.

They learn a lesson. They learn that fighting is bad. They learn that sharing is good. They learn that friendship is more important than a light square. They play with the other blocks. They are happy again.

Anna and Ben are friends. They like to play together. One day, they go to the park with their moms. They see a big tree with red apples.

"Look, apples!" Anna says. "Can we pick some?"

"OK, but be careful," their moms say. "Don't climb too high."

Anna and Ben run to the tree. They find a low branch with two apples. They reach up and pull the apples. They are shiny and sweet.

"Yum, yum!" Ben says. "These are good apples."

"Let's share with our moms," Anna says. "They will be happy."

They run back to their moms. They give them each an apple.

"Thank you, Anna and Ben," their moms say. "You are very kind."

Anna and Ben smile. They are proud. They hug their moms. Then they go to play some more. They have a fun day at the park.

name_of_work: The Heart by Jill Alexander Essbaum
content: A clementine Of inclement climate Grows tart. A crocus Too stoic to open, Won't. Like an oyster That cloisters a spoil of pearls, Untouched-- The heart that's had Enough Stays shut. Source: Poetry (December 2009)

name_of_work: On Easter Day by Oscar Wilde
content: The silver trumpets rang across the Dome: The people knelt upon the ground with awe: And borne upon the necks of men I saw, Like some great God, the Holy Lord of Rome. Priest-like, he wore a robe more white than foam, And, king-like, swathed himself in royal red, Three crowns of gold rose high upon his head: In splendour and in light the Pope passed home. My heart stole back across wide wastes of years To One who wandered by a lonely sea, And sought in vain for any place of rest: 'Foxes have holes, and every bird its nest, I, only I, must wander wearily, And bruise my feet, and drink wine salt with tears.'

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lucy. She loved to make things. Every day she would gather rocks and sticks and use them to make all sorts of wonderful things. 

One day, Lucy was in the garden. She looked around and noticed a beautiful big green tree. She wanted to make something special with the green tree! 

Lucy asked her Mom, "Mommy, can I make something special with the green tree?"

Mom answered, "Yes Lucy, that is a great idea. Just be sure to be careful and important so you don't hurt yourself."

So Lucy started making a beautiful green tree house. She and her friends had so much fun playing in it. Every day they would play games, tell stories and pretend they were living in a castle.

The green tree house was important to Lucy and her friends. They knew it was special and would always make sure to take care of it so they could always have a place to play and have fun.

Once there was a little boy named Bob. Bob had a rake and he liked to rake the leaves. But one day, Bob got a sour face when he started to rake. 

He said to himself, "This is too hard. I'm just gonna quit!" 

Just then, his mom walked into the yard. She said, "Bob, why quit? You can do this!" 

Bob thought for a minute, then he got a brave face. He said, "I'm gonna try again". 

So Bob tried and tried, and he didn't quit. Soon the leaves were all raked up and Bob was proud of himself. 

He said to his mom, "I did it! I didn't quit!" His mom said, "That's right! I knew you could do it!"
