Once upon a time, there was a wise owl who loved pizza. One day, the owl decided to make a pizza for lunch. She put the pizza in the oven to cook. But, she got distracted and forgot about the pizza. The pizza started to burn and the owl was sad. She knew she had to be more careful next time. The end.

Once upon a time there was a little girl called Sara. She was three years old and she was so excited, because it was her birthday! 

That morning, her mum and dad sung "Happy Birthday" to her and gave her a big surprise. It was a special doll with all the clothes and accessories Sara could wish for. Sara was so happy she couldn't contain her joy and hugged her mum and dad to thank them.

After that, Sara went to the park with her mum and dad and she had so much fun. She ran around, laughed and played with her doll. But then it started raining and that made Sara very miserable. She was sad and she wanted to go home. 

Her mum and dad said it was time to go and they took her home. Even though the rain had made Sara miserable, she still thanked them for taking her to the park to enjoy her birthday. 

And the mama and papa thanked Sara for being such a good girl, even on a rainy day.

Once upon a time there were two friends called June and Dave. They wanted to play a game, so June said, "Let's hide and see who finds who first!" Dave was excited and said, "Yes! I like hide and seek." 

June said, "I will close my eyes, and you go hide." Dave ran away to find a place to hide. Soon June opened her eyes and started to search for her friend. She looked in the garden and behind the trees. She asked the birds, "Have you seen Dave?" 

Finally,Dave shouted "Yes! I'm here." He came out from behind a big bush and said, "June, I found a rich spot! Look at all these amazing treasures." June was happy to see Dave, and they both laughed and hugged. 

"Let's play again tomorrow," said Dave. June agreed and said, "Yes, I can't wait for our next game!"

name_of_work: I Am a Little World Made Cunningly by John Donne
content: I am a little world made cunningly Of elements and an angelic sprite, But black sin hath betray'd to endless night My world's both parts, and oh both parts must die. You which beyond that heaven which was most high Have found new spheres, and of new lands can write, Pour new seas in mine eyes, that so I might Drown my world with my weeping earnestly, Or wash it, if it must be drown'd no more. But oh it must be burnt; alas the fire Of lust and envy have burnt it heretofore, And made it fouler; let their flames retire, And burn me O Lord, with a fiery zeal Of thee and thy house, which doth in eating heal.

Lily liked penguins very much. She had a toy penguin that she hugged every night. She also had a book about penguins that she read with her mom. She wanted to see real penguins, but they lived very far away.

One day, Lily went to the library with her mom. She saw a big poster of a penguin on the wall. She ran to it and pointed. "Mom, look! A penguin!" she said.

"Yes, that's a penguin," her mom said. "Do you want to borrow a book about penguins?"

Lily nodded. She followed her mom to the shelf where the books about animals were. She saw many books with pictures of penguins on the cover. She wanted to borrow them all.

"Mom, can I borrow this one? And this one? And this one?" she asked, holding up three books.

Her mom smiled. "You can only borrow two books at a time, Lily. You have to choose which ones you like best."

Lily frowned. She liked all the books. She did not want to choose. She was persistent. She held on to the books and said, "But I want all of them!"

Her mom shook her head. "You can't have all of them, Lily. Other children want to read them too. You have to share. How about you borrow one book today, and another one next week?"

Lily thought for a moment. She looked at the books. She decided to borrow the book with the biggest penguin on the cover. She gave the other two books to her mom. "OK, I will borrow this one today, and another one next week," she said.

Her mom praised her. "That's very good, Lily. You are a smart and kind girl. Let's go and check out the book, and then we can read it together at home."

Lily smiled. She was happy. She hugged her book and her toy penguin. She could not wait to learn more about penguins.

At the end of the day, Annabelle said to her parents, â€œI had a wonderful day. Thank you for taking me to the museum. Can we come back again soon?â€

Her parents laughed and smiled. â€œOf course we can come back,â€ her dad said. Annabelle was so happy and smiled from ear to ear.

Tom and Lily like to design things with their toys. They have blocks, cars, dolls, and animals. They make houses, roads, parks, and farms. They have fun playing together.

One day, they find a rat in their toy box. The rat is fat and brown. It has a long tail and sharp teeth. It scares Tom and Lily. They scream and run away.

"Mom! Mom! There is a rat in our toys!" Tom cries.

"Where? Where?" Mom asks. She comes to their room and sees the rat. She is not scared. She picks up the rat and holds it.

"Don't worry, kids. This is not a real rat. It is a toy rat. See? It has a button on its belly. If you press it, it makes a noise." Mom says. She presses the button and the rat squeaks.

Tom and Lily look at the rat. They see the button. They hear the noise. They are not scared anymore. They are curious.

"Can we play with the rat, Mom?" Lily asks.

"Sure, why not? It is a toy, like your other animals. You can design a home for it, or a friend, or a story." Mom says.

Tom and Lily smile. They take the rat and go back to their toys. They design a cage for the rat with their blocks. They give it some food and water. They make a hat for it with a doll's dress. They name it Ratty.

They have fun playing with Ratty. They forget that they were scared. They like their new toy. They thank Mom for finding it. Mom is happy to see them happy. She hugs them and kisses them. She loves them.

Lisa liked to help Mommy in the kitchen. She liked to choose what to eat for dinner. She liked to mix and stir and taste the food. She liked to make it delicious.

One day, Mommy said, "Lisa, today you can choose what to eat for dinner. What do you want?"

Lisa thought hard. She liked many things. She liked pizza and pasta and soup and salad. She liked chicken and fish and cheese and eggs. She liked fruit and cake and ice cream and cookies. But what did she want most?

She looked in the fridge and saw a big bowl of spaghetti. She looked in the cupboard and saw a jar of sauce. She looked in the drawer and saw a cheese grater. She smiled.

"I want spaghetti and cheese and sauce!" she said.

"Good choice, Lisa!" Mommy said. "That is easy and yummy. Let's make it together."

They boiled the water and cooked the spaghetti. They heated the sauce and poured it over the spaghetti. They grated the cheese and sprinkled it on top. They put the plates and forks and spoons on the table. They washed their hands and sat down to eat.

"Mmm, this is delicious!" Lisa said.

"I agree, this is delicious!" Mommy said. "You are a good helper and a good chooser, Lisa. Thank you for helping me in the kitchen."

Lisa felt happy and proud. She ate all her spaghetti and cheese and sauce. She helped Mommy put the dishes in the dishwasher. She gave Mommy a big hug and a kiss.

"I love you, Mommy," she said.

"I love you, Lisa," Mommy said. "You are my sweet and smart girl."

Once upon a time, there was a small boy named Timmy. He had a small toy car that he loved to play with. One day, he wanted to play with his car but he couldn't find it.

He asked his mom, "Mommy, where is my car?" His mom replied, "I don't know, Timmy. Did you put it in your toy box?" Timmy said, "No, I didn't. Can you help me find it?"

His mom said, "Sure, let's look for it together." They searched all over the house but couldn't find it. Finally, they found it locked in a small box. Timmy's mom had to use a key to unlock the box and Timmy was so happy to see his small toy car again.

That night your great guns, unawares, Shook all our coffins as we lay, And broke the chancel window-squares, We thought it was the Judgment-day And sat upright. While drearisome Arose the howl of wakened hounds: The mouse let fall the altar-crumb, The worms drew back into the mounds, The glebe cow drooled. Till God called, "No; It's gunnery practice out at sea Just as before you went below; The world is as it used to be: "All nations striving strong to make Red war yet redder. Mad as hatters They do no more for Christes sake Than you who are helpless in such matters. "That this is not the judgment-hour For some of them's a blessed thing, For if it were they'd have to scour Hell's floor for so much threatening.... "Ha, ha. It will be warmer when I blow the trumpet (if indeed I ever do; for you are men, And rest eternal sorely need)." So down we lay again. "I wonder, Will the world ever saner be," Said one, "than when He sent us under In our indifferent century!" And many a skeleton shook his head. "Instead of preaching forty year," My neighbour Parson Thirdly said, "I wish I had stuck to pipes and beer." Again the guns disturbed the hour, Roaring their readiness to avenge, As far inland as Stourton Tower, And Camelot, and starlit Stonehenge.

name_of_work: Effort at Speech Between Two People by Muriel Rukeyser
content: : Speak to me. Take my hand. What are you now? I will tell you all. I will conceal nothing. When I was three, a little child read a story about a rabbit who died, in the story, and I crawled under a chair : a pink rabbit : it was my birthday, and a candle burnt a sore spot on my finger, and I was told to be happy. : Oh, grow to know me. I am not happy. I will be open: Now I am thinking of white sails against a sky like music, like glad horns blowing, and birds tilting, and an arm about me. There was one I loved, who wanted to live, sailing. : Speak to me. Take my hand. What are you now? When I was nine, I was fruitily sentimental, fluid : and my widowed aunt played Chopin, and I bent my head on the painted woodwork, and wept. I want now to be close to you. I would link the minutes of my days close, somehow, to your days. : I am not happy. I will be open. I have liked lamps in evening corners, and quiet poems. There has been fear in my life. Sometimes I speculate On what a tragedy his life was, really. : Take my hand. Fist my mind in your hand. What are you now? When I was fourteen, I had dreams of suicide, and I stood at a steep window, at sunset, hoping toward death : if the light had not melted clouds and plains to beauty, if light had not transformed that day, I would have leapt. I am unhappy. I am lonely. Speak to me. : I will be open. I think he never loved me: He loved the bright beaches, the little lips of foam that ride small waves, he loved the veer of gulls: he said with a gay mouth: I love you. Grow to know me. : What are you now? If we could touch one another, if these our separate entities could come to grips, clenched like a Chinese puzzle . . . yesterday I stood in a crowded street that was live with people, and no one spoke a word, and the morning shone. Everyone silent, moving. . . . Take my hand. Speak to me.

name_of_work: On A Portrait Of A Deaf Man by Sir John Betjeman
content: The kind old face, the egg-shaped head, The tie, discretely loud, The loosely fitting shooting clothes, A closely fitting shroud. He liked old city dining rooms, Potatoes in their skin, But now his mouth is wide to let The London clay come in. He took me on long silent walks In country lanes when young. He knew the names of ev'ry bird But not the song it sung. And when he could not hear me speak He smiled and looked so wise That now I do not like to think Of maggots in his eyes. He liked the rain-washed Cornish air And smell of ploughed-up soil, He liked a landscape big and bare And painted it in oil. But least of all he liked that place Which hangs on Highgate Hill Of soaked Carrara-covered earth For Londoners to fill. He would have liked to say goodbye, Shake hands with many friends, In Highgate now his finger-bones Stick through his finger-ends. You, God, who treat him thus and thus, Say "Save his soul and pray." You ask me to believe You and I only see decay.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl who loved her daddy very much. Every day she would run to him when he arrived home, and give him the biggest hug.

On this day, the girl's daddy was not smiling. He was very sad and he just sat down on the couch and sighed. The girl wanted to make her daddy feel better, so she grabbed a furry blanket and wrapped it around her daddy's shoulders.

Her daddy looked down at the girl, and his face lit up with a smile. He scooped her up in his arms and chuckled. Daddy thanked his daughter for her kind gesture and the girl was so happy to make her daddy feel better.

The girl hugged her daddy tightly and said, "I love you, Daddy!" With one more sigh of contentment, Daddy hugged his daughter back, and the girl knew that Daddy was now happy again.

Tom and Lily were twins who liked to play outside. One day, they saw a big hill near their house. They wanted to climb the hill and see what was on the other side.

"Let's go, Lily!" Tom said. "Maybe we can find a treasure or a castle!"

"OK, Tom!" Lily said. "But we have to be careful and honest. We can't lie to Mom and Dad about where we are going."

They put on their coats and boots and ran to the hill. They started to climb, holding hands and helping each other. The hill was steep and slippery, but they were brave and strong.

As they climbed higher, they saw a white cloud around them. It was mist, and it made everything look fuzzy and soft. They could not see the top of the hill or the other side.

"Wow, Tom, this is so cool!" Lily said. "It's like we are in a fairy tale!"

"I know, Lily, it's amazing!" Tom said. "But we have to be careful. We don't want to get lost in the mist."

They kept climbing, but they did not find any treasure or castle. They only found more mist and rocks and grass. They started to feel cold and tired and hungry.

"Tom, I think we should go back," Lily said. "We have been climbing for a long time, and we don't know where we are."

"You're right, Lily," Tom said. "We have to be honest and tell Mom and Dad what we did. Maybe they will not be mad if we say we are sorry."

They turned around and started to climb down the hill. The mist was still thick, but they followed their footsteps and held hands. They hoped they would find their way back home.

name_of_work: Tears, Idle Tears by Alfred Lord Tennyson
content: Tears, idle tears, I know not what they mean, Tears from the depth of some divine despair Rise in the heart, and gather to the eyes, In looking on the happy Autumn-fields, And thinking of the days that are no more. Fresh as the first beam glittering on a sail, That brings our friends up from the underworld, Sad as the last which reddens over one That sinks with all we love below the verge; So sad, so fresh, the days that are no more. Ah, sad and strange as in dark summer dawns The earliest pipe of half-awaken'd birds To dying ears, when unto dying eyes The casement slowly grows a glimmering square; So sad, so strange, the days that are no more. Dear as remember'd kisses after death, And sweet as those by hopeless fancy feign'd On lips that are for others; deep as love, Deep as first love, and wild with all regret; O Death in Life, the days that are no more!

name_of_work: What Has Happened to Lulu? by Charles Causley
content: What has happened to Lulu, mother? What has happened to Lu? There's nothing in her bed but an old rag-doll And by its side a shoe. Why is her window wide, mother, The curtain flapping free, And only a circle on the dusty shelf Where her money-box used to be? Why do you turn your head, mother, And why do tear drops fall? And why do you crumple that note on the fire And say it is nothing at all? I woke to voices late last night, I heard an engine roar. Why do you tell me the things I heard Were a dream and nothing more? I heard somebody cry, mother, In anger or in pain, But now I ask you why, mother, You say it was a gust of rain. Why do you wander about as though You don't know what to do? What has happened to Lulu, mother? What has happened to Lu?

The moment she died, my mother's dance dresses turned from the colours they really were to the colours I imagine them to be. I can feel the weight of bumptoed silver shoes swinging from their anklestraps as she swaggers up the path towards her dad, light-headed from airman's kisses. Here, at what I'll have to learn to call my father's house, yes every ragbag scrap of duster prints her even more vivid than an Ilford snapshot on some seafront in a white cardigan and that exact frock. Old lipsticks. Liquid stockings. Labels like Harella, Gor-ray, Berketex. As I manhandle whole outfits into binbags for Oxfam every mote in my eye is a utility mark and this is useful: the sadness of dispossessed dresses, the decency of good coats roundshouldered in the darkness of wardrobes, the gravitas of lapels, the invisible danders of skin fizzing off from them like all that life that will not neatly end.

name_of_work: Lapis Lazuli by W. B. Yeats
content: I have heard that hysterical women say They are sick of the palette and fiddle-bow, Of poets that are always gay, For everybody knows or else should know That if nothing drastic is done Aeroplane and Zeppelin will come out, Pitch like King Billy bomb-balls in Until the town lie beaten flat. All perform their tragic play, There struts Hamlet, there is Lear, That's Ophelia, that Cordelia; Yet they, should the last scene be there, The great stage curtain about to drop, If worthy their prominent part in the play, Do not break up their lines to weep. They know that Hamlet and Lear are gay; Gaiety transfiguring all that dread. All men have aimed at, found and lost; Black out; Heaven blazing into the head: Tragedy wrought to its uttermost. Though Hamlet rambles and Lear rages, And all the drop scenes drop at once Upon a hundred thousand stages, It cannot grow by an inch or an ounce. On their own feet they came, or on shipboard, Camel-back, horse-back, ass-back, mule-back, Old civilisations put to the sword. Then they and their wisdom went to rack: No handiwork of Callimachus Who handled marble as if it were bronze, Made draperies that seemed to rise When sea-wind swept the corner, stands; His long lamp chimney shaped like the stem Of a slender palm, stood but a day; All things fall and are built again And those that build them again are gay. Two Chinamen, behind them a third, Are carved in Lapis Lazuli, Over them flies a long-legged bird A symbol of longevity; The third, doubtless a serving-man, Carries a musical instrument. Every discolouration of the stone, Every accidental crack or dent Seems a water-course or an avalanche, Or lofty slope where it still snows Though doubtless plum or cherry-branch Sweetens the little half-way house Those Chinamen climb towards, and I Delight to imagine them seated there; There, on the mountain and the sky, On all the tragic scene they stare. One asks for mournful melodies; Accomplished fingers begin to play. Their eyes mid many wrinkles, their eyes, Their ancient, glittering eyes, are gay.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. He loved to eat yummy cookies that his mommy made. One day, Timmy's mommy promised him that if he ate all his vegetables, they would celebrate by baking his favorite cookies. Timmy was so happy and ate all his veggies. 

When dinner was over, Timmy's mommy kept her promise and they started to bake the cookies together. Timmy helped his mommy mix the dough and put it in the oven. While they waited for the cookies to bake, they danced and sang together. 

Finally, the cookies were ready! Timmy's mommy took them out of the oven and they both ate them while they hugged each other. Timmy was so happy that they celebrated their promise by baking his favorite yummy cookies. From that day on, Timmy always ate his veggies so they could celebrate with cookies again.

Once upon a time there was a mum and a dad. They wanted to show their daughter something special. So they took her outside to a field full of flowers. Looking up they showed her a big lightbulb that lit up the night sky. The little girl was so excited, she asked what it was. The dad said it was very interesting - it was called a 'bulb'. 

The little girl wanted to stay and look at the bulb for as long as she could, so mum and dad agreed. They lay down on the grass and just watched the bulb at night. The little girl thought it was so beautiful and asked questions about it. Dad explained that the bulb stayed lit all night and made the darkness go away. 

The little girl was so happy she just wanted to stay in the field forever. But it was getting late and soon it was time for bed. As she went off to sleep, the little girl said she wanted to come back and stay with the bulb again.

Once upon a time, there was a happy figure. Her name was Eva and she loved to spend time outside. Every day she would swing on the swing set and go for nature walks. 

One day, she found a special spot in the mountains. She was so enthusiastic! She decided to spend the whole day exploring it. She hiked up and down the trails, she played hide and seek in the trees, and she made silly shapes in the clouds. 

Before she knew it, the sun had already set. She was so eager to get back home, so she ran as fast as she could back to her house. She waved goodbye to the mountains and promised to come back another day. 

Eva learned so many things that day. Being enthusiastic always makes the day more special and spending time with nature is the best way to make new friends.

Once upon a time, there was a monkey. The monkey lived in a big tree in the jungle. One day, the monkey saw a man walking by. The man was carrying a big bag. The monkey asked the man, "What do you have in your bag?" The man replied, "I have some unusual things in my bag. I work at the circus and these things are for the show."

The monkey was curious and asked the man if he could see the unusual things. The man agreed and showed the monkey some juggling balls and a unicycle. The monkey was amazed and asked the man if he could try them out. The man said yes and the monkey started to juggle the balls and ride the unicycle.

The man was surprised and said, "You are a very talented monkey! Would you like to come work at the circus with me?" The monkey thought about it and said, "Yes, I would love to work at the circus!" And so, the monkey left the jungle and joined the circus, where he became a star performer.

Once upon a time there was a little boy named Jake. Jake was very curious and liked to explore his world. One day Jake went to visit his grandma's ranch. While he was there, he saw something very strange. There were a lot of people wiping weird things off the walls and doors. He asked his grandma what was going on and she told him they were cleaning up the ranch.

Jake was surprised! He had never seen anyone clean before. He asked his grandma why there was so much dirt and she explained that the ignorant people who came before him had left it there. They had not taken care of the ranch like she did.

Jake wanted to help clean too. He grabbed a rag and started wiping some of the dirt away. He wiped for hours, until the ranch was clean. Grandma was proud of him and gave him a hug. He was proud of himself too! From then on he always tried to help keep the ranch clean and teach other kids to do the same.

You may talk o' gin and beer When you're quartered safe out 'ere, An' you're sent to penny-fights an' Aldershot it; But when it comes to slaughter You will do your work on water, An' you'll lick the bloomin' boots of 'im that's got it. Now in Injia's sunny clime, Where I used to spend my time A-servin' of 'Er Majesty the Queen, Of all them blackfaced crew The finest man I knew Was our regimental bhisti, Gunga Din, He was 'Din! Din! Din! 'You limpin' lump o' brick-dust, Gunga Din! 'Hi! Slippy hitherao 'Water, get it! Panee lao, 'You squidgy-nosed old idol, Gunga Din.' The uniform 'e wore Was nothin' much before, An' rather less than 'arf o' that be'ind, For a piece o' twisty rag An' a goatskin water-bag Was all the field-equipment 'e could find. When the sweatin' troop-train lay In a sidin' through the day, Where the 'eat would make your bloomin' eyebrows crawl, We shouted 'Harry By!' Till our throats were bricky-dry, Then we wopped 'im 'cause 'e couldn't serve us all. It was 'Din! Din! Din! 'You 'eathen, where the mischief 'ave you been? 'You put some juldee in it 'Or I'll marrow you this minute 'If you don't fill up my helmet, Gunga Din!' 'E would dot an' carry one Till the longest day was done; An' 'e didn't seem to know the use o' fear. If we charged or broke or cut, You could bet your bloomin' nut, 'E'd be waitin' fifty paces right flank rear. With 'is mussick on 'is back, 'E would skip with our attack, An' watch us till the bugles made 'Retire,' An' for all 'is dirty 'ide 'E was white, clear white, inside When 'e went to tend the wounded under fire! It was 'Din! Din! Din!' With the bullets kickin' dust-spots on the green. When the cartridges ran out, You could hear the front-ranks shout, 'Hi! ammunition-mules an' Gunga Din!' I shan't forgit the night When I dropped be'ind the fight With a bullet where my belt-plate should 'a' been. I was chokin' mad with thirst, An' the man that spied me first Was our good old grinnin', gruntin' Gunga Din. 'E lifted up my 'ead, An' he plugged me where I bled, An' 'e guv me 'arf-a-pint o' water green. It was crawlin' and it stunk, But of all the drinks I've drunk, I'm gratefullest to one from Gunga Din. It was 'Din! Din! Din! ''Ere's a beggar with a bullet through 'is spleen; ''E's chawin' up the ground, 'An' 'e's kickin' all around: 'For Gawd's sake git the water, Gunga Din!' 'E carried me away To where a dooli lay, An' a bullet come an' drilled the beggar clean. 'E put me safe inside, An' just before 'e died, 'I 'ope you liked your drink,' sez Gunga Din. So I'll meet 'im later on At the place where 'e is gone-- Where it's always double drill and no canteen. 'E'll be squattin' on the coals Givin' drink to poor damned souls, An' I'll get a swig in hell from Gunga Din! Yes, Din! Din! Din! You Lazarushian-leather Gunga Din! Though I've belted you and flayed you, By the livin' Gawd that made you, You're a better man than I am, Gunga Din!

Sara and Ben were playing outside with their new ball. They liked to kick the ball and catch it and throw it. They had a lot of fun with their ball.

But then the sky became dark and the wind blew hard. They heard a loud noise and saw a big flash. It was a storm. They were scared and ran inside the house.

They looked out the window and saw the rain falling. They wanted the storm to go away. They wanted to play with their ball again.

"Look, Sara, look!" Ben said. He pointed at the sky. "There is a rainbow!"

Sara looked and saw the rainbow. It had many colors. It was pretty. She smiled.

"Maybe the rainbow will make the storm go away," she said. "Maybe we can go outside soon."

They waited and watched the rainbow. They hoped it would stay.

But then they heard another loud noise and saw another big flash. It was a bigger storm. They saw the rain falling harder. They saw the wind blowing stronger. They saw the rainbow fading.

They saw their ball flying away.

They cried and cried. They lost their ball. They lost their rainbow. They lost their fun.

The storm did not go away. It spoiled their day. It spoiled their ball. It spoiled their rainbow.

They could not restore their ball. They could not restore their rainbow. They could not restore their fun.

They were sad and angry. They did not like the storm. They did not like the rain. They did not like the wind.

They did not like anything.

Max and his mom were walking in the park. Max saw a big body on the ground with an arm and a leg sticking up. He was afraid and he grabbed his mom's hand. His mom said, "It's okay, Max. That's just a hurt body that needs help." They walked closer and saw that it was a hurt bird. Max's mom said, "Let's help her!" They carefully picked up the body and took it to the animal hospital. The doctor gave the bird a pill and said, "Welcome back my feathered friend!" Max gave the bird a kiss on the head and said, "Welcome back!" The bird flew away and Max and his mom watched as it soared up into the sky.

Living in the earth-deposits of our history Today a backhoe divulged out of a crumbling flank of earth one bottle amber perfect a hundred-year-old cure for fever or melancholy a tonic for living on this earth in the winters of this climate. Today I was reading about Marie Curie: she must have known she suffered from radiation sickness her body bombarded for years by the element she had purified It seems she denied to the end the source of the cataracts on her eyes the cracked and suppurating skin of her finger-ends till she could no longer hold a test-tube or a pencil She died a famous woman denying her wounds denying her wounds came from the same source as her power.

name_of_work: A Song About Myself by John Keats
content: I. There was a naughty boy, A naughty boy was he, He would not stop at home, He could not quiet be- He took In his knapsack A book Full of vowels And a shirt With some towels, A slight cap For night cap, A hair brush, Comb ditto, New stockings For old ones Would split O! This knapsack Tight at's back He rivetted close And followed his nose To the north, To the north, And follow'd his nose To the north. II. There was a naughty boy And a naughty boy was he, For nothing would he do But scribble poetry- He took An ink stand In his hand And a pen Big as ten In the other, And away In a pother He ran To the mountains And fountains And ghostes And postes And witches And ditches And wrote In his coat When the weather Was cool, Fear of gout, And without When the weather Was warm- Och the charm When we choose To follow one's nose To the north, To the north, To follow one's nose To the north! III. There was a naughty boy And a naughty boy was he, He kept little fishes In washing tubs three In spite Of the might Of the maid Nor afraid Of his Granny-good- He often would Hurly burly Get up early And go By hook or crook To the brook And bring home Miller's thumb, Tittlebat Not over fat, Minnows small As the stall Of a glove, Not above The size Of a nice Little baby's Little fingers- O he made 'Twas his trade Of fish a pretty kettle A kettle- A kettle Of fish a pretty kettle A kettle! IV. There was a naughty boy, And a naughty boy was he, He ran away to Scotland The people for to see- There he found That the ground Was as hard, That a yard Was as long, That a song Was as merry, That a cherry Was as red, That lead Was as weighty, That fourscore Was as eighty, That a door Was as wooden As in England- So he stood in his shoes And he wonder'd, He wonder'd, He stood in his Shoes and he wonder'd.

Sara loves her new switch. It is red and shiny and makes a click sound when she pushes it. She likes to play with it in her room and see what it does. Sometimes it turns on a light, sometimes it makes a noise, sometimes it does nothing.

One day, Sara hears a knock on her door. It is her friend Ben. He wants to play with her. Sara is happy to see him and invites him in. She shows him her new switch and tells him how much she loves it. Ben thinks it looks fun and asks if he can try it.

Sara says yes and lets him push the switch. But when he does, something bad happens. The switch makes a loud boom and sparks fly out of it. Sara and Ben are scared and jump back. They smell smoke and see a small fire on the wall. They scream and run out of the room.

Sara's mom hears them and comes to see what is wrong. She sees the fire and grabs a bucket of water. She throws the water on the fire and puts it out. She is angry and asks Sara and Ben what they did. Sara tells her about the new switch and how Ben pushed it. Sara's mom says the switch was not a toy, it was a part of the old heater that was broken. She says Sara should not have played with it or let Ben touch it. She says it was very dangerous and could have hurt them or burned the house.

Sara feels sorry and says she did not know. She says she loves her mom and does not want to make her mad. She says she is sorry to Ben too and hopes he is not mad at her. Ben says he is not mad, he is just glad they are okay. He says he loves Sara too and they are still friends. Sara's mom hugs them both and says she loves them too. She says she is glad they are okay too, but they have to be more careful and not play with things they do not understand. She says she will get Sara a new toy switch that is safe and fun. Sara and Ben smile and say thank you. They promise to be more careful and listen to Sara's mom. They go to play with Sara's other toys and wait for the new switch.

Once upon a time, there was a little bunny named Benny. Benny loved to talk to his friends and family. He would talk about all sorts of things like the weather and what he ate for lunch. One day, Benny heard some news that made him sad. His friend, the squirrel, had lost his acorn collection. Benny wanted to help his friend, so he talked to the other animals in the forest. They all worked together to find the missing acorns and return them to the squirrel. It took a long time, but they finally found them all! Benny learned that when he talks to others and works together, he can help make things better.

Once, there was a stubborn pilot. He recorded all the things he saw from the sky in his special notebook. He flew in his plane over the mountains, rarely stopping.

One day, his plane ran low on fuel and he had to land in a valley. He looked around for help but none came. He was very stubborn and didn't want to stay there.

The pilot noticed an old man walking by and asked him for help. The old man smiled and said he would find some fuel for him. The pilot was so happy to see that the man had kept his word.

The old man helped the pilot record everything he had seen in the sky. They both talked and laughed, and when the pilot finished recording, he thanked the man and flew away in his plane.

Though the stubborn pilot was far away, he never forgot the old manâ€™s kindness. Whenever he flew higher and higher into the sky, he felt the old manâ€™s help pushing him along.

Lily loved her stuff. She had a lot of stuff in her room. She had dolls and books and cars and balls and puzzles and crayons. She liked to play with her stuff every day. She hugged her stuff and said nice things to them.

One day, Lily's mom said they had to go to the store. Lily wanted to bring some of her stuff with her. She picked her favorite doll, a book, and a car. She hugged them and put them in her backpack. She was ready to go.

At the store, Lily saw a lot of new stuff. She saw toys and clothes and food and candy. She wanted to look at everything. She asked her mom if she could have some of the stuff. Her mom said no, they had enough stuff at home.

Lily was sad. She wanted more stuff. She saw a big teddy bear that was very jolly. It had a red bow and a smile. She wanted to hug it and take it home. She reached for it, but her mom stopped her.

"Lily, you can't have that. That's not yours. That's the store's stuff. You have to pay for it if you want it. And we don't have money for that. Come on, let's go."

Lily was very sad. She cried and cried. She didn't want to leave the teddy bear. She wanted to hug it and make it her stuff. She didn't understand why she couldn't have it.

Her mom hugged her and said, "I'm sorry, Lily. I know you like the teddy bear. But you have a lot of stuff at home that loves you. And I love you too. You don't need more stuff to be happy. You just need hugs and love. Do you understand?"

Lily nodded. She wiped her tears and smiled. She hugged her mom and said, "I love you, mom. And I love my stuff. Thank you for taking me to the store. Can we go home now?"

Her mom smiled and said, "Yes, we can go home now. Let's go, Lily."

Lily took her backpack and held her mom's hand. She was happy again. She had her stuff and her mom. She didn't need more stuff. She had enough.

Tom and Anna were playing in the park. They liked to run, jump and slide on the grass and the swings. They saw a big hill with many flowers and trees. They wanted to climb the hill and see what was on the other side.

"Let's go, Tom!" Anna said. "Maybe we can find something fun!"

"OK, Anna!" Tom said. "But we have to be careful. The hill is high and steep."

They held hands and started to rise the hill. They went slowly and stopped to look at the flowers and the birds. They saw a yellow butterfly and a red ladybug. They smiled and waved at them.

When they reached the top of the hill, they saw a big lake with many ducks and fish. They also saw a small house with a fence and a garden. They wondered who lived there.

"Look, Tom!" Anna said. "There is a house! Maybe we can say hello!"

"OK, Anna!" Tom said. "But we have to be polite. Maybe they are busy or tired."

They walked to the house and knocked on the door. A kind old lady opened the door and smiled at them.

"Hello, children!" she said. "What are you doing here?"

"Hello, lady!" Anna said. "We are playing in the park. We rose the hill and saw your house. We wanted to say hello!"

"Hello, lady!" Tom said. "We are sorry to bother you. We are just curious. We like your house and your garden!"

The old lady laughed and invited them in. She gave them some cookies and milk and told them stories about the lake and the animals. She was very generous and friendly.

"Thank you, lady!" Anna said. "You are very nice and sweet!"

"Thank you, lady!" Tom said. "You are very kind and fun!"

They hugged the old lady and said goodbye. They walked back to the park and continued to play. They were happy and grateful. They had a wonderful day.

name_of_work: Out of the Bag by Seamus Heaney
content: All of us came in Doctor Kerlin's bag. He'd arrive with it, disappear to the room And by the time he'd reappear to wash Those nosy, rosy, big, soft hands of his In the scullery basin, its lined insides (The colour of a spaniel's inside lug) Were empty for all to see, the trap-sprung mouth Unsnibbed and gaping wide. Then like a hypnotist Unwinding us, he'd wind the instruments Back into their lining, tie the cloth Like an apron round itself, Darken the door and leave With the bag in his hand, a plump ark by the keel ... Until the next time came and in he'd come In his fur-lined collar that was also spaniel-coloured And go stooping up to the room again, a whiff Of disinfectant, a Dutch interior gleam Of waistcoat satin and highlights on the forceps. Getting the water ready, that was next-- Not plumping hot, and not lukewarm, but soft, Sud-luscious, saved for him from the rain-butt And savoured by him afterwards, all thanks Denied as he towelled hard and fast, Then held his arms out suddenly behind him To be squired and silk-lined into the camel coat. At which point he once turned his eyes upon me, Hyperborean, beyond-the-north-wind blue, Two peepholes to the locked room I saw into Every time his name was mentioned, skimmed Milk and ice, swabbed porcelain, the white And chill of tiles, steel hooks, chrome surgery tools And blood dreeps in the sawdust where it thickened At the foot of each cold wall. And overhead The little, pendent, teat-hued infant parts Strung neatly from a line up near the ceiling-- A toe, a foot and shin, an arm, a cock A bit like the rosebud in his buttonhole. Poeta doctus Peter Levi says Sanctuaries of Asclepius (called asclepions) Were the equivalent of hospitals In ancient Greece. Or of shrines like Lourdes, Says poeta doctus Graves. Or of the cure By poetry that cannot be coerced, Say I, who realized at Epidaurus That the whole place was a sanatorium With theatre and gymnasium and baths, A site of incubation, where "incubation" Was technical and ritual, meaning sleep When epiphany occurred and you met the god ... Hatless, groggy, shadowing myself As the thurifer I was in an open air procession In Lourdes in '56 When I nearly fainted from the heat and fumes, Again I nearly fainted as I bent To pull a bunch of grass and hallucinated Doctor Kerlin at the steamed-up glass Of our scullery window, starting in to draw With his large pink index finger dot-faced men With button-spots in a straight line down their fronts And women with dot breasts, giving them all A set of droopy sausage-arms and legs That soon began to run. And then as he dipped and laved In the generous suds again, miraculum: The baby bits all came together swimming Into his soapy big hygienic hands And I myself came to, blinded with sweat, Blinking and shaky in the windless light. Bits of the grass I pulled I posted off To one going into chemotherapy And one who had come through. I didn't want To leave the place or link up with the others. It was mid-day, mid-May, pre-tourist sunlight In the precincts of the god, The very site of the temple of Asclepius. I wanted nothing more than to lie down Under hogweed, under seeded grass And to be visited in the very eye of the day By Hygeia, his daughter, her name still clarifying The haven of light she was, the undarkening door. The room I came from and the rest of us all came from Stays pure reality where I stand alone, Standing the passage of time, and she's asleep In sheets put on for the doctor, wedding presents That showed up again and again, bridal And usual and useful at births and deaths. Me at the bedside, incubating for real, Peering, appearing to her as she closes And opens her eyes, then lapses back Into a faraway smile whose precinct of vision I would enter every time, to assist and be asked In that hoarsened whisper of triumph, "And what do you think Of the new wee baby the doctor brought for us all When I was asleep?"

The Ocean has its silent caves, Deep, quiet, and alone; Though there be fury on the waves, Beneath them there is none. The awful spirits of the deep Hold their communion there; And there are those for whom we weep, The young, the bright, the fair. Calmly the wearied seamen rest Beneath their own blue sea. The ocean solitudes are blest, For there is purity. The earth has guilt, the earth has care, Unquiet are its graves; But peaceful sleep is ever there, Beneath the dark blue waves.

Sara likes to rise early and look at the sky. She likes to see the colors of the sun and the clouds. Sometimes she sees birds and planes too. She likes to dream of flying with them.

One morning, Sara woke up and saw only gray. The sky was gray, the clouds were gray, and the sun was hidden. She felt sad and bored. She did not want to dream of flying in the gray sky.

She went to her mom and said, "Mom, why is the sky gray? Where is the sun? Where are the birds and the planes?"

Her mom hugged her and said, "Don't worry, Sara. The sky is gray because it is going to rain. The sun is behind the clouds, and the birds and the planes are hiding. But the rain will not last long. Soon the sky will be blue again, and the sun will shine, and the birds and the planes will come out. Then you can dream of flying with them again."

Sara smiled and said, "Thank you, mom. I like the rain too. It makes the flowers grow and the earth smell good. Can we go outside and play in the rain?"

Her mom nodded and said, "Yes, we can. But first, let's have some breakfast. You need to eat well to fly high."

Sara and her mom ate some toast and jam, and then put on their raincoats and boots. They went outside and played in the rain. Sara saw a rainbow in the sky and felt happy. She still dreamed of flying, but she also enjoyed the rain.

By channels of coolness the echoes are calling, And down the dim gorges I hear the creek falling; It lives in the mountain, where moss and the sedges Touch with their beauty the banks and the ledges; Through brakes of the cedar and sycamore bowers Struggles the light that is love to the flowers. And, softer than slumber, and sweeter than singing, The notes of the bell-birds are running and ringing. The silver-voiced bell-birds, the darlings of day-time, They sing in September their songs of the May-time. When shadows wax strong and the thunder-bolts hurtle, They hide with their fear in the leaves of the myrtle; When rain and the sunbeams shine mingled together They start up like fairies that follow fair weather, And straightway the hues of their feathers unfolden Are the green and the purple, the blue and the golden. October, the maiden of bright yellow tresses, Loiters for love in these cool wildernesses; Loiters knee-deep in the grasses to listen, Where dripping rocks gleam and the leafy pools glisten. Then is the time when the water-moons splendid Break with their gold, and are scattered or blended Over the creeks, till the woodlands have warning Of songs of the bell-bird and wings of the morning. Welcome as waters unkissed by the summers Are the voices of bell-birds to thirsty far-comers. When fiery December sets foot in the forest, And the need of the wayfarer presses the sorest, Pent in the ridges for ever and ever. The bell-birds direct him to spring and to river, With ring and with ripple, like runnels whose torrents Are toned by the pebbles and leaves in the currents. Often I sit, looking back to a childhood Mixt with the sights and the sounds of the wildwood, Longing for power and the sweetness to fashion Lyrics with beats like the heart-beats of passion -- Songs interwoven of lights and of laughters Borrowed from bell-birds in far forest rafters; So I might keep in the city and alleys The beauty and strength of the deep mountain valleys, Charming to slumber the pain of my losses With glimpses of creeks and a vision of mosses.

Once upon a time, there was a gentle mama rabbit. She had a nest in the woods and every morning she'd take a walk through the trees. One day while she was out walking, she saw something shiny in the grass. She stopped to take a closer look and saw it was a trap! She hopped back, scared.

Suddenly, she heard someone calling her. It was her baby bunny, who had been watching her from the nest. He wanted to explore the trap and see if it was safe. Mama rabbit shook her head, but she also knew that he was curious. So she let him go over to the trap and gently showed him how to stay away from it's sharp teeth.

Finally, Mama Rabbit said it was time for baby bunny to go back home. He said goodbye, and hopped away. Mama Rabbit watched him and smiled. She knew he was safe and happy, and would remember what she had taught him.

Once upon a time, there was a giant. The giant was very big and very alert. She could hear everything around her! She watched the world go by and listened to the birds chirping in the trees. 

One day, she decided to take a nap. As she fell asleep, she began to imagine a far away land filled with adventure and excitement. In her dream, she flew through the sky and visited exciting places.

When the giant awoke, she felt more alert than before. She realized that she could make her dreams a reality. With a little bit of courage, she was able to go to those exciting places she had dreamed about. 

The end.

Once upon a time, there was an elephant in a long field. His name was Edward and he was very happy. One day, Edward wanted to manage something, but he didn't know what.

Just then, a butterfly flew near him. "Hello!", said the butterfly.

Edward was very excited. "Hello!", he said back.

"Have you ever managed anything before?" asked the butterfly.

Edward thought for a moment. "No, I haven't," he replied.

The butterfly smiled. "Well why don't you try managing this field? The grass is really tall and it needs to be cut down."

Edward thought it was a great idea. He spread his trunk wide, and managed to cut the tall grass down to make it clear. 

When he was done, Edward looked around and smiled. He had managed the field perfectly! He was so proud of himself.

"Well done Edward!" said the butterfly, flying away. 

Edward was so happy that he gave a trumpet of joy!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved going on adventures with her family. One day, they went on a trip to a big house in the woods. When they got there, they had to unpack all their things from the car.

Lily noticed something strange about the house. It had a mystery feeling to it. She asked her mom and dad, but they didn't know what she meant. They just said it was an old house.

As they explored the house, they found an old chest. It looked like it had been there for a long time. Lily was curious and wanted to open it, but her dad said it was locked and they didn't have the key.

Later that night, they all went to bed. But Lily couldn't sleep. She wanted to know what was in the chest. So she snuck out of bed and went to find it. She found the key and opened the chest. But inside, there was nothing but an old, grumpy ghost. The ghost scared Lily so much that she ran back to her room and hid under the covers. From that day on, Lily was too scared to go on any more adventures.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play outside with his friends. One day, Timmy's mom asked him to prepare for a picnic. Timmy was excited and asked his mom what he needed to do. 

His mom told him to get a cap because it was going to be sunny outside. Timmy found his favorite blue cap and put it on his head. Then, his mom asked him to help prepare the sandwiches. Timmy found it difficult to spread the peanut butter on the bread, but he tried his best. 

After they finished preparing the sandwiches, Timmy and his family went to the park for a picnic. They ate the sandwiches, played games, and had a lot of fun. Timmy was happy that he helped prepare for the picnic and wore his cap the whole time.

Once upon a time, there was a worried owl. The owl lived in a big tree. The tree was in a pretty forest.

One day, the owl saw a small door on the tree. The door was open. The owl was worried. He did not know who opened the door. So, the owl wanted to close the door.

The owl used his wing to close the door. The door was now closed. The owl was happy. He was not worried anymore. The owl went to sleep in his big tree.

Lila and Sam were restless. They did not want to nap. They wanted to play. They looked at the window and saw the wild birds. They had bright colors and loud songs. They flew from tree to tree.

"Let's go outside and see the birds!" Lila said to Sam.

"OK, but we have to be quiet. Mom is sleeping," Sam said.

They put on their shoes and jackets and opened the door. They ran to the backyard. They saw the birds on the fence and the grass. They tried to get closer, but the birds flew away.

"Come back, birds! We want to be your friends!" Lila shouted.

"Shh, Lila! You are scaring them!" Sam whispered.

They saw a birdhouse on a pole. It had a hole and a perch. They saw a blue bird inside. It looked at them with its black eyes.

"Maybe this bird will let us play with it," Lila said.

She took a chair from the patio and set it under the pole. She climbed on the chair and reached for the birdhouse.

"Be careful, Lila! You might fall!" Sam said.

But Lila did not listen. She grabbed the birdhouse and pulled it down. The blue bird flew out and squawked. It pecked Lila's hand and made her cry.

"Ow, ow, ow! The bird bit me!" Lila wailed.

Sam ran to her and hugged her. He saw blood on her hand. He was scared.

"Mom, mom, mom! Help!" He yelled.

Mom heard the noise and woke up. She ran to the backyard and saw Lila and Sam. She saw the birdhouse on the ground and the blue bird flying away.

"What happened here?" She asked.

"Lila wanted to play with the bird, but the bird was wild and bit her," Sam said.

Mom took Lila's hand and cleaned it. She put a band-aid on it and kissed it.

"It's OK, Lila. The bird was scared and angry. You should not touch wild animals. They need their space and their home," Mom said.

"I'm sorry, Mom. I just wanted to see the bird," Lila said.

"I know, Lila. But you have to be gentle and respectful with nature. And you have to listen to Sam. He was trying to help you," Mom said.

"I'm sorry, Sam. You were right. I was not careful," Lila said.

"It's OK, Lila. I'm glad you are OK. I love you," Sam said.

They hugged each other and said sorry. Mom smiled and hugged them too.

"Come on, let's go inside and have some cookies. And then you can nap. You must be tired after your adventure," Mom said.

Lila and Sam nodded and followed Mom. They learned their lesson and decided to watch the birds from the window next time.

Once upon a time, there were two friends called Sarah and Jack. They were always together, going on adventures and having fun.

One day, Sarah had a surprise for Jack. She asked him to close his eyes and not look until she said so. Eagerly, Jack closed his eyes and waited.

"You can open them now!" Sarah said cheerfully.

Jack opened his eyes to find a small present in front of him. He was so excited to see what it was! He opened it up and inside he found a toy car. Jack thanked Sarah, but then made a foolish request.

"Can I have another one?" he asked.

Sarah smiled. "That's not very nice, Jack. You have to be content with the surprise I gave you!" Jack knew she was right, so he thanked her again and hugged his new toy car.

Lily and Tom are in the car with Mom. They are going to the park. But there is a lot of traffic on the road. The cars are not moving fast. They are moving slow. Lily and Tom are bored.

"Mom, when will we get to the park?" Lily asks.

"Soon, honey. We just have to wait a little bit more," Mom says.

Tom looks out the window. He sees a big truck. The truck has a picture of a dog on it. The dog is smiling. Tom likes the dog.

"Look, Lily, a dog!" Tom says.

Lily looks out the window too. She sees the dog. She likes the dog too.

"Can we pet the dog, Mom?" Lily asks.

"No, sweetie. The dog is not real. It is just a picture on the truck," Mom says.

Lily and Tom are sad. They want to pet a real dog.

Suddenly, they hear a loud honk. The truck behind them has bumped into their car. Mom is surprised. She stops the car. She gets out to talk to the truck driver.

"Are you okay, Mom?" Lily asks.

Mom comes back to the car. She gives Lily and Tom a hug. She says they are brave.

"Can we still go to the park, Mom?" Tom asks.

Lily and Tom are happy. They rub the dirt off the car with Mom. Then they drive to the park. They hope to see a real dog. They hope the dog will let them pet it. They hope the dog will not be clumsy.

name_of_work: Rhyme of the Dead Self by A.R.D. Fairburn
content: Tonight I have taken all that I was and strangled him pale that lily white lad. I have choked him with these my hands these claws catching him as he lay a-dreaming in his bed. Then chuckling I dragged out his foolish brains that were full of pretty love-tales heighho the holly. And emptied them holus bolus to the drains those dreams of love oh what ruinous folly. He is dead pale youth and he shall not rise on the third day or any other day sloughed like a snakeskin there he lies and he shall not trouble me again for aye.

Once upon a time, there was an old lady. She loved to watch movies. But she didn't have any movies to watch. She asked her friend to provide her with a movie. Her friend was happy to help and gave her an old movie. The old lady was very happy and watched the movie all day long. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Anna. She was very curious and always wanted to explore new things. 

One day, Anna went to her first class. She was very excited and looked around. She could see many strange and unusual things. Anna gazed around in amazement, taking in all the new sights, sounds, and smells.

Suddenly, Anna heard a funny noise coming from behind her. She spun around and saw a big brown dog staring at her. Anna smiled and the dog barked in response. 

They became friends and the dog followed Anna to class. Everyone stared in surprise and amusement, but the teacher was not too happy. 

The teacher said, "The classroom is no place for pets. It's best if you leave him outside," and Anna had to say goodbye to her new companion.

Anna was very sad, but she realized that rules were in place for a reason. She learned that it was important to always follow the rules, no matter how unusual they may seem.

Once upon a time, there was a bald man called Jack. One day, Jack was walking in the woods and he came across a big barrel that was broken. He noticed that it was full of apples.

Jack smiled and said: "Oh! A barrel! I can repair this barrel for my apples."

name_of_work: The Mountain And The Squirrel by Ralph Waldo Emerson
content: The mountain and the squirrel Had a quarrel, And the former called the latter "Little prig." Bun replied, "You are doubtless very big; But all sorts of things and weather Must be taken in together To make up a year And a sphere. And I think it no disgrace To occupy my place. Anna and Ben were twins who liked to play with fire. They had a box of matches that they stole from their dad. They would sneak out to the backyard and light things on fire, like leaves, sticks and paper. They thought it was fun to watch the flames and the smoke.

One day, they found a big pile of wood that their dad had chopped for the winter. They decided to make a huge fire with it. They piled up the wood and lit a match. The fire grew very fast and very hot. It made a lot of ash that flew in the air. Anna and Ben were scared and ran away.

The fire was so big that it reached the tall tree next to the house. The tree caught fire and the fire spread to the roof. The house was on fire too. Anna and Ben saw the fire from the street and cried. They saw their mom and dad come out of the house. They were angry and sad.

"Anna! Ben! What have you done?" their mom shouted. "You could have burned the whole house down! You could have hurt yourselves and us! How could you be so foolish and dangerous?"

"We're sorry, mom. We're sorry, dad. We didn't mean to. We just wanted to play with fire. We didn't know it would be so bad." Anna and Ben said.

"You didn't know? You didn't know that fire can burn and destroy and hurt? You didn't know that you should never play with fire or matches? You didn't know that you should listen to us and obey us?" their dad said.

"No, we didn't know. We were stupid. We were bad. We're sorry. We're sorry. We're sorry." Anna and Ben said.

Their mom and dad hugged them and said, "We're glad you're safe. We're glad we're safe. But you have to learn from your mistake. You have to be careful and responsible. You have to respect fire and life. You have to pray and ask God to forgive you and help you."

Anna and Ben nodded and said, "We will, mom. We will, dad. We will pray and ask God to forgive us and help us. We will never play with fire or matches again. We love you, mom. We love you, dad."

They all prayed together and thanked God for saving them. They looked at the house and saw the firemen putting out the fire. They saw the ash and the damage. They felt sad but also grateful. They learned a hard lesson that day. They learned to never play with fire.

name_of_work: The Vanity Of Wealth by Samuel Johnson
content: No more thus brooding o'er yon heap, With avarice painful vigils keep: Still unenjoy'd the present store, Still endless sighs are breathed for more. O! quit the shadow, catch the prize, Which not all India's treasure buys! To purchase with heaven has gold the power? Can gold remove the mortal hour? In life can love be bought with gold? Are friendship's pleasures to be sold? No! - all that's worth a wish - a thought, Fair virtue gives unbribed, unbought, Cease then on trash thy hopes to bind, Let noble views engage thy mind. With science tread the wondrous way, Or learn the Muses' moral lay; In social hours indulge thy soul, Where mirth and temperance mix the bowl; To virtuous love resign thy breast, And be, by blessing beauty, - bless'd. Thus taste the feast by Nature spread, Ere youth and all its joys are fled; Come taste with me the balm of life, Secure from pomp, and wealth, and strife. I boast whate'er for man was meant, In health, and Stella, and content; And scorn! (oh! let that scorn be thine!) Mere things of clay, that dig the mine.

Once upon a time there lived a bald man. He always sat and watched a flame. He liked to sit and watch it for hours, feeling the warm and peaceful light on his skin.

name_of_work: The Haunted Palace by Edgar Allan Poe
content: In the greenest of our valleys By good angels tenanted, Once a fair and stately palace-- Radiant palace--reared its head. In the monarch Thought's dominion, It stood there! Never seraph spread a pinion Over fabric half so fair! Banners yellow, glorious, golden, On its roof did float and flow (This--all this--was in the olden Time long ago) And every gentle air that dallied, In that sweet day, Along the ramparts plumed and pallid, A winged odor went away. Wanderers in that happy valley, Through two luminous windows, saw Spirits moving musically To a lute's well-tuned law, Round about a throne where, sitting, Porphyrogene! In state his glory well befitting, The ruler of the realm was seen. And all with pearl and ruby glowing Was the fair palace door, Through which came flowing, flowing, flowing And sparkling evermore, A troop of Echoes, whose sweet duty Was but to sing, In voices of surpassing beauty, The wit and wisdom of their king. But evil things, in robes of sorrow, Assailed the monarch's high estate; (Ah, let us mourn!--for never morrow Shall dawn upon him, desolate!) And round about his home the glory That blushed and bloomed Is but a dim-remembered story Of the old time entombed. And travellers, now, within that valley, Through the red-litten windows see Vast forms that move fantastically To a discordant melody; While, like a ghastly rapid river, Through the pale door A hideous throng rush out forever, And laugh--but smile no more.

name_of_work: When We Were Kids by Mario Benedetti
content: When we were kids Thirty sounded so old The pool was an ocean And death, plainly put, Did not exist. Then as teenagers Forty-somethings were the geezers, The pond was an ocean And death but A word. Later, when we got married, Fifty was old, The lake was an ocean And death was somebody Else's. Now, we the veterans Have finally gotten hold of truth The ocean being at last the ocean And death just becoming Ours.

Tim and Kim are twins. They like to play and have fun. But they do not like to eat their meals. They say they are not hungry or they do not like the food. Mom and Dad are sad and worried.

One day, Mom and Dad have an idea. They tell Tim and Kim that they can get a good meal if they do something nice for someone else. They can help a friend, a neighbor, or an animal. They can share, be kind, or be brave. They can choose what they want to do.

Tim and Kim think this is a fun game. They go out and look for someone to help. Tim sees a cat stuck in a tree. He climbs up and saves the cat. The cat is happy and purrs. Kim sees a girl who is sad because she lost her ball. She gives her one of her balls. The girl is happy and smiles.

Tim and Kim run back to Mom and Dad. They tell them what they did. Mom and Dad are proud and happy. They hug Tim and Kim and give them a good meal. Tim and Kim eat their food and say it is yummy. They learn that helping others makes them feel good and hungry. They decide to do something nice every day.

Once upon a time, there was a nosy rabbit named Benny. Benny always wanted to know what other animals were doing. One day, Benny saw a squirrel lifting a big pile of clothes. Benny wanted to know why the squirrel was lifting the clothes, so he asked the squirrel. The squirrel said he was helping his mom wash the clothes.

Benny thought that was a good idea, so he went home and asked his mom if he could help with the laundry too. His mom said yes, and Benny helped lift the clothes into the washing machine. After they were done washing, Benny helped lift the clothes out of the machine and put them in the dryer.

Benny learned that it's always good to help others and that sometimes, being nosy can lead to learning new things and helping out. From that day on, Benny always looked for ways to help his family and friends.

On a warm summer day, a caterpillar crawled up a tree. He was looking for a nice, quiet place to relax. As he climbed, he heard a lot of very noisy birds singing in the branches. It was too loud for him to relax, so he kept climbing. As he got higher and higher, the noise of the birds got quieter and quieter.

Soon, he found the perfect place - a big leaf of the tree - where he could relax in peace. He curled up and closed his eyes, soaking in the nice sunshine.

After resting a little bit, the caterpillar heard a different sound - a very gentle buzzing noise. He opened an eye and saw a few bees flying around the tree. They looked so peaceful, that the caterpillar decided to stay and relax. He lay down on the leaf and watched the busy bees buzzing around the tree. It felt so nice and peaceful, like he was part of the buzzing noise itself.

The caterpillar stayed there for hours until the sun started to set and the air was getting cooler. Finally, it was time to go home and the caterpillar slowly crawled back down the tree. He was relaxed and happy from a wonderful day spent in the tree.

She saw a mysterious pen with sparkles on it and asked her mommy if she could buy it. Her mommy said yes and they spent the whole day drawing together. Luna tried to open the can, but she could not. Then, her friend, a small bird named Tim, came to help. Tim said, "Let's measure the can to see how big it is."

Luna and Tim measured the can of tuna. They found out it was very big. Together, they worked hard to open it. Finally, the can was open, and Luna and Tim shared the tasty tuna. They were very happy and full.

name_of_work: No Master by William H. Davies
content: Indeed this is the sweet life! my hand Is under no proud man's command; There is no voice to break my rest Before a bird has left its nest; There is no man to change my mood, When I go nutting in the wood; No man to pluck my sleeve and say -- I want thy labour for this day; No man to keep me out of sight, When that dear Sun is shining bright. None but my friends shall have command Upon my time, my heart and hand; I'll rise from sleep to help a friend, But let no stranger orders send, Or hear my curses fast and thick, Which in his purse-proud throat would stick Like burrs. If I cannot be free To do such work as pleases me, Near woodland pools and under trees, You'll get no work at all, for I Would rather live this life and die A beggar or a thief, than be A working slave with no days free.

name_of_work: Christmas Comes to Moccasin Flat by James Welch
content: Christmas comes like this: Wise men unhurried, candles bought on credit (poor price for calves), warriors face down in wine sleep. Winds cheat to pull heat from smoke. Friends sit in chinked cabins, stare out plastic windows and wait for commodities. Charlie Blackbird, twenty miles from church and bar, stabs his fire with flint. When drunks drain radiators for love or need, chiefs eat snow and talk of change, an urge to laugh pounding in their ribs. Elk play games in high country. Medicine Woman, clay pipe and twist tobacco, calls each blizzard by name and predicts five o'clock by spitting at her television. Children lean into her breath to beg a story. Something about honor and passion, warriors back with meat and song, a peculiar evening star, quick vision of birth. Blackbird feeds his fire. Outside, a quick thirty below.

Once upon a time, there was a yellow crane. The crane lived in a big city and loved to perform. One day, the crane went to the park to perform for the children. 

The children were so excited to see the yellow crane perform. But then, a mean dog came and started to bark at the crane. The crane was scared and didn't want to perform anymore. 

A little boy saw that the crane was scared and said, "Don't worry, yellow crane. I'll protect you from the mean dog. You can still perform for us." The crane felt better and started to perform again. The children clapped and cheered for the yellow crane. The crane was happy and grateful to the little boy who helped him.

Once upon a time, there was a popular dog named Spot. Spot was very friendly and loved to play with all the other dogs. One day, Spot went to the park to play, but it was very cold outside. Spot did not mind the cold because he had a warm coat of fur.

While playing in the park, Spot saw a little dog shivering from the cold. Spot felt bad for the little dog and wanted to help. So, Spot shared his warm fur by standing close to the little dog. The little dog stopped shivering and they both played happily together.

Later, Spot did something silly and felt embarrass. But the little dog reminded Spot of how he helped him when he was cold. Spot learned that it's okay to feel embarrass sometimes, because true friends will always remember the good things you do. The moral of the story is to always be kind and help others, even when it's cold outside.

content: You ask me what I mean by saying I have lost my tongue. You could not use them both together even if you thought that way. And if you lived in a place you had to speak a foreign tongue, your mother tongue would rot, rot and die in your mouth until you had to spit it out. name_of_work: O that 'twere possible by Alfred Lord Tennyson
content: O that 'twere possible After long grief and pain To find the arms of my true love Round me once again!... A shadow flits before me, Not thou, but like to thee: Ah, Christ! that it were possible For one short hour to see The souls we loved, that they might tell us What and where they be!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside and collect rocks. One day, while she was looking for rocks, she met a boy named Max.

Max said, "Hi! What are you doing?"

"I'm looking for rocks," Lily said.

"I'm good at finding rocks," Max said. "I'm gifted."

Lily was impressed. "Wow! Can you show me?"

Max nodded and they started looking for rocks together. They found a big, shiny rock and Max said, "This one is special. It's like a gift!"

Lily smiled. "Can I keep it?"

"Sure!" Max said. "Let's put it in your pocket." Lily zipped up her pocket and they continued looking for more rocks. They had so much fun together that they became friends and went rock hunting every day.

Tim and Lily were friends who liked to play outside. One day, they found a place with many flowers and trees. They saw a bird with long wings and bright colors. The bird was hurt and could not fly.

"Look, a bird!" Tim said. "It is so pretty. I want to keep it."

"No, Tim. The bird is sad. It needs to go back to its home in the sky." Lily said. "We should help it."

They gently picked up the bird and put it in a box. They took it to their house and gave it some water and seeds. They made a soft bed for it with some cloth. They raised the box to the window so the bird could see the sun.

Every day, they checked on the bird and talked to it. The bird started to feel better and chirp. Tim and Lily were happy, but they also knew they had to let the bird go.

One morning, they opened the window and the box. The bird looked at them and sang a song. Then it spread its long wings and flew away. Tim and Lily waved goodbye and smiled.

They learned that sometimes the best way to love something is to set it free. They also learned that helping others can make them happy too. They were proud of themselves and their new friend.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl who wanted to explore the world. One day, she saw a mineral that was glowing brightly. She got excited and wanted to poke it to see what would happen.

The mineral was magical, and started to move around! She tried to poke it again, but it was too fast for her. She chased it all around the room, but it moved too quick. Soon enough, she was so tired and had to give up.

All of a sudden, a wise old man walked into the room and saw what was happening. He asked the little girl why she was being so ignorant and trying to poke the mineral.

The little girl was embarrassed and stopped to think. She realised that she had been silly and that she should be more respectful of the world around her. The wise old man smiled at her and said that she had learned something very important that day.

The little girl thanked the wise old man for his help. From then on, she was always careful not to make the same mistake again and to be more respectful of her surroundings.

name_of_work: A Child to his Sick Grandfather by Joanna Baillie
content: Grand-dad, they say you're old and frail, Your stocked legs begin to fail: Your knobbed stick (that was my horse) Can scarce support your bended corse; While back to wall you lean so sad, I'm vexed to see you, dad. You used to smile and stroke my head, And tell me how good children did; But now, I wot not how it be, You take me seldom on your knee; Yet ne'ertheless I am right glad To sit beside you, dad. How lank and thin your beard hangs down! Scant are the white hairs on your crown; How wan and hollow are your cheeks! Your brow is rough with crossing breaks; But yet, for all his strength is fled, I love my own old dad. The housewives round their potions brew, And gossips come to ask for you: And for your weal each neighbour cares, And good men kneel, and say their pray'rs: And ev'rybody looks so sad, When you are ailing, dad. You will not die, and leave us then? Rouse up and be our dad again. When you are quiet and laid in bed, We'll doff our shoes and softly tread: And when you wake we'll aye be near, To fill old dad his cheer. When through the house you shift your stand, I'll lead you kindly by the hand; When dinner's set, I'll with you bide, And aye be serving by your side; And when the weary fire burns blue, I'll sit and talk with you. I have a tale both long and good, About a partlet and her brood; And cunning greedy fox that stole, By dead of midnight, through a hole, Which slyly to the hen-roost led -- You love a story, dad? And then I have a wond'rous tale Of men all clad in coats of mail, With glitt'ring swords -- you nod, I think? Your fixed eyes begin to wink; Down on your bosom sinks your head; You do not hear me, dad.

Anna and Ben love to play music. They have a band with their toys. Anna plays the drum and Ben plays the guitar. They sing loud and have fun.

One day, they see a big poster on the wall. It shows a real band with many people and instruments. They look impressive. They wear shiny clothes and have big smiles. The poster says they will play at the park tomorrow.

"Wow, look at that band!" Anna says. "They are so cool!"

"I want to see them!" Ben says. "Can we go to the park tomorrow, please?"

Anna and Ben ask their mom if they can go to the park. Their mom says yes, but they have to be good and do their chores. Anna and Ben agree. They do their chores and go to bed early.

The next day, they go to the park with their mom. They see many people and hear loud music. They see the band on a big stage. They play the guitar, the drum, the piano, the trumpet and the violin. They sing and dance and make everyone happy.

Anna and Ben are amazed. They clap and cheer. They want to be like them.

When the band finishes, they say thank you and bow. Then they come down from the stage and walk among the people. They give hugs and autographs and smiles.

Anna and Ben are excited. They run to the band and say hello. They tell them they love their music and they have a band too.

The band is surprised and happy. They ask Anna and Ben what they play. Anna and Ben show them their toys. The band laughs and says they are cute.

Then the band does something amazing. They kneel down and play with Anna and Ben. They use their toys and make music together. They sing and have fun.

Anna and Ben are so happy. They feel like they are part of the band. They hug the band and say thank you.

The band says they are welcome. They say Anna and Ben are impressive. They say they have talent and they should keep playing.

Anna and Ben smile and say they will. They say goodbye to the band and go home with their mom. They are proud and happy. They have a band with their toys and their friends. They play music and have fun.

Once upon a time, there was a brave rabbit who lived in the bush. One day he was feeling very brave and decided to hop around the bush. He suddenly saw a very big bee and became scared. As he tried to run away, he and the bee bumped into each other. The bee got angry, and the rabbit was scared he was going to get stung. The rabbit tried to apologize, but the bee wouldn't listen. The bee eventually flew away, and instead of being brave, the rabbit stayed in the bush and regretted his choice. Fortunately for the rabbit, he never ever saw the bee again!

One day, a little bird woke up early to see the sunrise. It was very pretty. The bird saw an ugly bug on a leaf. The bird said, "Hi, bug! Do you want to see the sunrise with me?"

The bug said, "Yes, I want to see the sunrise too. But I can't fly like you. Can you help me get up high?" The bird thought about it and had an idea.

The bird told the bug, "Hold on to my leg, and I will fly you up high to see the sunrise." The bug held on tight, and the bird flew up high. They saw the pretty sunrise together. The bird and the bug became good friends, and they knew they would have many more fun days together.

They both had beautiful ideas, but they could not agree.

One day, Betty said, â€œLetâ€™s have a contest and the winner gets a victory.â€
