Harry was an eager 3 year old who loved getting his back rubbed. He would just sit there for hours and enjoy feeling the massage on his tiny body.

Today, Harry was in the kitchen looking for his mom. For some reason, she had not been able to give him his massage today.

"Mom," Harry said, "can I still have a massage today?"

His mom looked down at her sleepy little son and smiled.

"Of course you can, honey," she said as she started rubbing his back.

Harry felt the warm massage on his back and smiled. He was so happy that he had gotten his massage today. He wanted to feel this massage every single day. He was so eager to feel the warmth and the comfort that this massage provided.

After Harry was done with his massage, he gave his mother a big hug and thanked her. His mom smiled and said that it was her pleasure.

Harry ran off to play and enjoy the rest of his day, feeling relaxed and content.

Molly and Sally were best friends and they loved to play together. One day, they decided to have a big adventure. Molly took all her special clothes out of the wardrobe and layed them on the floor. 

Sally said, "Let's destroy your clothes - it will be fun!"

Molly smiled. "Okay," she said.

Molly and Sally hopped around and threw all the normal clothes in the air. They laughed as the clothes floated and twirled above them. 

When they were done, Molly and Sally had made a huge mess. All the clothes were in a big pile. 

Molly said, "That was so much fun!"

Sally nodded. "Let's do it again!" she said. 

So Molly and Sally went to find more normal clothes to destroy.

Once there was a little girl named Jane. Jane loved colors and every day she would explore her world in search of new colors. One day as she was walking, Jane noticed a clear river. She decided to have a closer look and as she approached, her eyes widened in amazement. The river was full of different colors! Jane was so excited that she jumped into the river and began to swim.

Jane was quickly introduced to all the beautiful colors of the river, from yellows and oranges to blues and greens. She had never seen such a wonderful place in all her life!

Jane swam for hours, playing and enjoying the colors of the river. When it was time to go, Jane smiled and waved goodbye to the river, grateful for the new colors she had been introduced to.

Sam and Mia were twins who loved to play at the beach. They liked to build sand castles, find shells, and splash in the water. One day, they saw a big bottle on the shore. It was green and shiny, and had a cork on top.

"Look, Mia, a bottle!" Sam said. "Maybe there is a message inside!"

"Let's open it, Sam!" Mia said. They pulled the cork and heard a hiss. A cloud of smoke came out of the bottle, and a voice said, "Thank you for freeing me! I am a genie, and I will grant you one wish each!"

Sam and Mia were amazed and excited. They had never seen a genie before. They thought about what they wanted to wish for.

"I wish for a beautiful dress!" Mia said. She loved to dress up and look pretty.

"Your wish is granted!" the genie said. He snapped his fingers, and Mia was wearing a beautiful dress. It was pink and sparkly, and had a bow on the back.

"Wow, Mia, you look beautiful!" Sam said.

"Thank you, Sam!" Mia said. She twirled and smiled.

"What do you wish for, Sam?" the genie asked.

Sam thought for a moment. He liked to explore and have adventures. He looked at the sea and saw the tide coming in.

"I wish for a drink of the tide!" Sam said. He was curious about how the water tasted.

"Your wish is granted!" the genie said. He snapped his fingers, and Sam had a cup of water in his hand. It was salty and bitter.

"Yuck, Sam, why did you wish for that?" Mia asked.

"I wanted to try it, Mia!" Sam said. He took a sip and made a face. "It's not good, Mia! It's bad!"

Sam and Mia learned a lesson that day. They learned that some things are better to look at than to drink. They learned to be careful what they wish for. They thanked the genie and went back to playing at the beach. They had fun with their sand castles, shells, and water. They were happy with what they had.

name_of_work: Symptoms of Love by Robert Graves

Take courage, lover! Could you endure such pain At any hand but hers?

Once upon a time, there was a little fish named Fin. Fin loved to swim in the wild sea with his friends. They would play all day long in the warm water.

One day, Fin saw a big boat. He wanted to ask the boat to play with him. Fin swam up to the boat and said, "Please, can you play with me?" The boat did not say anything, but it moved a little in the water.

Fin was very happy. He swam back to his friends and told them about the big boat. They all swam together and played with the boat. It was a fun day for Fin and his friends in the wild sea.

Lily and Ben were twins who liked to play together. They had many toys, but their favorite was a big box of socks. They liked to make sock puppets and put on shows for their mom and dad.

One day, they found a new sock in the box. It was red and green and had a shiny star on it. Lily and Ben both wanted to use it for their puppet. They started to pull on the sock and argue.

"Let go, it's mine!" Lily said.

"No, it's mine!" Ben said.

They pulled harder and harder, until the sock ripped in half. They both felt sad and sorry. They looked at the torn sock and then at each other.

"I'm sorry, Lily. I was mean to you. You can have the sock." Ben said.

"I'm sorry, Ben. I was mean to you too. You can have the sock." Lily said.

They hugged and said they were sorry again. Then they had an idea. They took the two halves of the sock and sewed them together. They made a new puppet that was red and green and had two shiny stars. They named it Starry.

They showed their mom and dad their new puppet. Mom and dad smiled and clapped. They said they were proud of Lily and Ben for being humble and sharing. They said they admired their creativity and kindness.

Lily and Ben felt happy and hugged their mom and dad. They thanked them for the sock and said they loved them. They put on a show with Starry and their other sock puppets. They had fun and laughed a lot. They learned that sharing is better than fighting.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lucy. Lucy loved to bake cakes with her mom. One day, Lucy decided to make a cake all by herself. She put on her apron and her glove, and started mixing the ingredients. But she accidentally put in too much salt and the cake tasted yucky.

Lucy was sad because she wanted the cake to be perfect. She didn't know what to do. But then, her mom came to help her. They mixed in some more sugar and flour, and the cake tasted much better. Lucy was happy again and she learned that it's okay to ask for help when things go wrong.

Once upon a time, there was a family of four who lived in a little cottage. One day in the fall, a sky man came down from the clouds and warned them about the winter. The sky man said winter was coming soon and it was going to be very cold.

The family panicked, for they were not prepared for the cold. They had no warm clothes or enough firewood to keep them warm. 

Just then, a big red truck pulled up. A kind lady stepped out of the truck and said, "I have heard the warnings and I am here to help. I have enough clothes and firewood to last you all the winter."

The family was so grateful for the kind lady's help. They thanked her and quickly started to get ready for winter. They put up their warm clothes and started making the firewood last until the end of winter. 

The family made it through the winter and were very grateful for the kind lady's help.  They lived happily ever since.

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Sarah. Every week, Sarah helped her mommy cook something fancy. This made Sarah so happy! 

First, they would chop the carrots, then they would make easy macarons. When it was time to bake the cake, they would measure the sugar and flour. 

When they were finished cooking they would lay the table with flowers and feathers. They would put on their best dress and enjoy their fancy dinner together. 

Every week, Sarah would help her mommy cook something special. This made them both very happy.

Once upon a time, there was a wide carpet that could talk. It lived in a little girl's room. The little girl, named Lily, loved to play on the carpet. One day, Lily asked the carpet, "Why are you so wide?" The carpet replied, "I am wide so that you and your friends can play on me."

One day, Lily's friend, Tim, came over to play. They played with their toys on the wide carpet. Tim accidentally spilled juice on the carpet. Lily got upset and said, "Now my carpet is dirty!" The carpet replied, "It's okay, I can be cleaned."

Lily's mom helped clean the carpet. Lily and Tim said sorry to the carpet. The carpet replied, "It's okay, just remember to be careful next time." The moral value of the story is to always say sorry when you make a mistake and to learn from it.

Davey was playing in his bedroom one day and he saw something shiny on the floor. He went over to investigate. It was a cute, little nail. He thought it would be fun to use it. 

Davey picked up the nail and ran over to his toy box. He put the nail on the shelf and started pounding it into the wood with a large, plastic hammer. His mom walked in and was startled by the noise. 

"Davey, what are you doing?" his mom asked.

"Mommy, I'm using this cute nail!" Davey said, pointing to the nail sticking out of the toy box.

"Oh, ok," his mom said, giving him a smile. She saw that her son was having lots of fun and she enjoyed watching him play. From then on, Davey always used his nail to make his toys better.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with cardboard boxes. One day, Lily's mom gave her a big box to play with. It was smooth and shiny, and Lily loved it.

Lily played with the box all day, making a fort and a castle. But when it was time for bed, she didn't put the box away. Instead, she scattered it all over the floor.

The next day, Lily's mom tripped on the cardboard and fell. She hurt her knee and had to go to the hospital. Lily felt very bad. She realized that she should have put the cardboard away. From then on, Lily always put her toys away so that nobody would trip and get hurt.

name_of_work: To a Blank Sheet of Paper by Oliver Wendell Holmes
content: WAN-VISAGED thing! thy virgin leaf To me looks more than deadly pale, Unknowing what may stain thee yet,-- A poem or a tale. Who can thy unborn meaning scan? Can Seer or Sibyl read thee now? No,--seek to trace the fate of man Write on his infant brow. Love may light on thy snowy cheek, And shake his Eden-breathing plumes; Then shalt thou tell how Lelia smiles, Or Angelina blooms. Satire may lift his bearded lance, Forestalling Time's slow-moving scythe, And, scattered on thy little field, Disjointed bards may writhe. Perchance a vision of the night, Some grizzled spectre, gaunt and thin, Or sheeted corpse, may stalk along, Or skeleton may grin! If it should be in pensive hour Some sorrow-moving theme I try, Ah, maiden, how thy tears will fall, For all I doom to die! But if in merry mood I touch Thy leaves, then shall the sight of thee Sow smiles as thick on rosy lips As ripples on the sea. The Weekly press shall gladly stoop To bind thee up among its sheaves; The Daily steal they shining ore, To gild its leaden leaves. Thou has no tonuge, yet thou canst speak, Till distant shores shall hear the sound; Thou hast no life, yet thou canst breathe Fresh life on all around. Thou art the arena of the wise, The noiseless battle-ground of fame; The sky where halos may be wreathed Around the humblest name. Take, then, this treasure to thy trust, To win some idle reader's smile, Then fade and moulder in the dust, Or swell some bonfire's crackling pile!

name_of_work: Lying in a Hammock at William Duffy's Farm in Pine Island, Minnesota by James Wright
content: Over my head, I see the bronze butterfly, Asleep on the black trunk, Blowing like a leaf in green shadow. To my right, In a field of sunlight between two pines, The droppings of last year's horses Blaze up into golden stones. I lean back, as the evening darkens and comes on. name_of_work: Down By the Salley Gardens by William Butler Yeats
content: Down by the salley gardens my love and I did meet; She passed the salley gardens with little snow-white feet. In a field by the river my love and I did stand, And on my leaning shoulder she laid her snow-white hand. Once upon a time there was a wealthy fairy named Sparkles. She loved to stand on her magical toe and twirl around in the air.
One day, Sparkles was standing in her garden, admiring the beauty of the trees and the flowers. Suddenly, a little 3 year old child appeared beside her. He asked, "Why do you stand here?"

Sparkles smiled and said, "I stand here because it makes me happy. I'm a wealthy fairy who loves to twirl around in the air and enjoy the beauty around me."
 
The little child was fascinated and asked, "Can I twirl in the air too?" Sparkles replied, "Of course you can! All you need to do is stand up on your own two feet, wave your arms and twirl around."
The little child did just that and soon he was twirling around the garden with Sparkles. 

The little 3 year old smiled, feeling the wind ruffle his hair and thanked Sparkles for the special gift. 

And from then on, anytime Sparkles visited the garden, the little child would join her, and twirl around together in the air. They were the best of friends.

Lily loved sugar. She liked to eat sugar on her bread, in her milk, and from the jar. She knew Mommy said no more sugar, but she did not listen. She was sneaky and took sugar when Mommy was not looking.

One day, Mommy went to the store and left Lily with Daddy. Lily saw the jar of sugar on the shelf and wanted some. She climbed on a chair and reached for the jar. But the jar was too heavy and she dropped it. The jar broke and sugar spilled everywhere. Lily was scared and guilty. She heard Daddy coming and hid under the table.

Daddy saw the mess and was angry. He looked for Lily and found her under the table. He pulled her out and yelled at her. He said she was naughty and had to go to her room. He did not hug her or kiss her. He did not say he loved her. He just sent her away.

Lily ran to her room and cried. She felt sad and lonely. She wished she had not taken the sugar. She wished Daddy would hug her and say he was sorry. She wished Mommy would come back and make everything better. But no one came. Lily stayed in her room and cried until she fell asleep. She had a bad dream about sugar and Daddy. She did not have a good day.

Once upon a time, there was a humble doctor. He was very kind and always helped people. One day, he saw a little girl who was hurt and very sad.

The doctor smiled at the little girl and said hello. She was so scared, but the doctor just whispered softly. He said kind things to her and eventually she stopped crying.

The doctor took care of the little girl and made sure she felt better. After a while, she was back to her happy self. She gave the doctor a big hug and thanked him before she went on her way.

The little girl was so grateful to the kind doctor. Every time she thought of him, she would whisper gentle thank yous to the sky.

Once upon a time there was a frog called Pete. Pete lived in an oasis. He loved swimming around and eating flies. One day, Pete decided to explore the oasis. He hopped around the oasis and eventually came to a big lake. 

As Pete went closer, he realised something was wrong. The water was not moving. It was completely still. He could not find any flies in the water either. Pete knew he had to do something. 

Suddenly, he remembered something he had heard from another frog. He quickly hopped back to his oasis and put some stones in the middle. Then, he hopped back to the big lake. 

The stones worked. The water began to move fast. Pete was delighted. He soon found many flies in the fast flowing water. Pete rejoiced in his oasis and was happy to explore new places.

name_of_work: I Dream'd in a Dream by Walt Whitman
content: I DREAM'D in a dream, I saw a city invincible to the attacks of the whole of the rest of the earth; I dream'd that was the new City of Friends; Nothing was greater there than the quality of robust love--it led the rest; It was seen every hour in the actions of the men of that city, And in all their looks and words.

The child saw a track in the sand. He wanted to follow it, so he started walking. On the track, he noticed something special. It was a compassionate animal. The animal was hurt and couldn't walk. The child saw this and felt sad. 

He wanted to help the animal so he got some water from a nearby stream. He carefully gave the water to the animal and it started to feel better. The animal drank for a few minutes then got up. He followed the child back home. 

The child was so happy! He was so compassionate and he was glad that he was able to help the animal. From that day on, that animal was the child's friend. They would meet every day and the child would take care of the animal.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, she went for a walk in the park with her mom. They saw a lady sitting on a bench. The lady looked very dry because it was a hot day.

Lily wanted to say hi to the lady, so she ran over to her. But she accidentally stumbled on a rock and fell down. The lady saw what happened and asked, "Are you okay?"

Lily's mom helped her up and said, "Yes, she's fine. Thank you for asking." The lady smiled and said, "Be careful, little one. The ground can be tricky sometimes." Lily nodded and said, "I will be careful next time." Then, she and her mom continued their walk in the park.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, she went to school and her teacher had a big blackboard. The blackboard was very big and black, and Lily liked it a lot. 

The teacher would talk to the class and write on the blackboard with white chalk. Sometimes, the teacher's voice was harsh and Lily would cover her ears. But other times, the teacher's voice was soft and Lily could hear everything clearly.

Lily loved going to school and seeing the big blackboard. She liked when the teacher would talk and write on it. And even though sometimes the teacher's voice was harsh, Lily knew that the teacher loved her and wanted her to learn.

Tom and Lily were playing in the park. They saw a big pond with many ducks and fish. They also saw a small otter swimming and diving in the water. The otter looked happy and playful.

"Look, Lily, an otter!" Tom said. "He is so cute and fast!"

"Can we pet him, Tom?" Lily asked.

"I don't know, Lily. He might be shy or scared of us. Let's watch him from here."

They sat on the grass and watched the otter for a while. They saw him catch a fish and eat it. They saw him splash and slide on the rocks. They saw him dig a hole and bury something in it.

"What is he burying, Tom?" Lily wondered.

"Maybe he is hiding his food or his toys. Otters like to bury things for later," Tom explained.

"Can we see what he buried, Tom?" Lily asked.

"Maybe, but we have to be careful and quiet. We don't want to scare him or make him angry," Tom said.

They waited until the otter swam away to another part of the pond. Then they walked slowly and softly to the hole. They looked inside and saw a shiny stone.

"Wow, a pretty stone!" Lily said. "It is blue and sparkly!"

"Maybe the otter found it and liked it. Maybe he wanted to keep it safe," Tom said.

"Can we take it, Tom?" Lily asked.

Tom thought for a moment. He liked the stone too, but he also liked the otter. He remembered that the otter was generous and shared his fish with the ducks. He decided to be generous too.

"No, Lily, we can't take it. It is the otter's stone. He buried it here for a reason. We should leave it alone," Tom said.

"Okay, Tom, you are right. The otter is nice and we should be nice too," Lily said.

They covered the hole with dirt and grass. They waved goodbye to the otter and thanked him for letting them see his stone. They went back to their mom and dad and told them about their adventure. They were happy and proud of being good friends to the otter.

Once upon a time there was a little boy named Dave. He was only three years old and he loved to ask questions. One day, Dave asked his big brother what a spell was. His brother explained that a spell was like a special word that could help you do something.

Dave then asked what the spell was. His brother said it was an older and more mysterious word, so he couldn't tell him. Dave knew that his brother was telling the truth so he didn't push it.

Instead, Dave asked his mom for help. She smiled and told him that the spell was a modest word and she would help him find it.

Together, mother and son searched through some books until they found the spell. Dave was so excited that he asked what it did. His mom said it was a special word that could make things happen.

Dave was so happy that he found the spell. He thanked his mom and ran off to show his brother the special word.

The End.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play dress up and pretend she was a princess. One day, she saw a painter outside her house. He was painting the walls of her neighbor's house. 

Lily went outside to say hello. "Hi, Mr. Painter! You are painting fast!" she said. The painter smiled and said, "Yes, I am trying to finish before it gets dark." 

Lily then asked, "Can you paint me too?" The painter laughed and said, "I don't think I can paint you, but I can paint a picture of you!" Lily was so happy and said, "Yay! I can't wait to see it!" 

The painter finished his work and gave Lily the picture. She was so excited and said, "Thank you, Mr. Painter! I will hang this up in my room!" And from that day on, Lily always remembered the kind painter who painted her picture fast.

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Claire. Claire was only three years old and she was the happiest girl around. One day, Claire was so excited to go outside for a little exercise. She raced outside with a big smile on her face.

Claire was feeling so good that she decided to bury something special too. She collected some stones and leaves, dug a big hole and put them inside. 

Claire's Mom watched from the patio and asked; "What did you bury, Claire?".

"It's a secret!", Claire said with a big grin.

After she was done, Claire continued on her way for some exercise. She skipped around the garden and ran down the street until she found a comfortable spot to sit and relax. Then, she noticed that there was something special in the ground next to her.

Claire dug the ground and she found the stones and leaves she buried earlier. She was so happy to see them again. Claire knew that she was special, just like the things she buried.

Claire was so happy she smiled and skipped back home - feeling comfortable and proud of her secret treasure.

Once upon a time, there was a little duck named Ducky. Ducky loved to swim in the pond with his friends. One day, Ducky saw some dark clouds in the sky. He knew it was going to rain soon. Ducky quickly waddled to his home to tell his family.

As Ducky arrived at his home, he saw that his head was wet from the rain. His mom and dad were happy that Ducky was safe from the rain. Ducky's siblings were also happy that he arrived home safely.

Ducky and his family snuggled together in their cozy home while the rain poured outside. Ducky was grateful that he had a warm place to stay while it rained.

The most important thing we've learned, So far as children are concerned, Is never, NEVER, NEVER let Them near your television set - Or better still, just don't install The idiotic thing at all. In almost every house we've been, We've watched them gaping at the screen. They loll and slop and lounge about, And stare until their eyes pop out. (Last week in someone's place we saw A dozen eyeballs on the floor.) They sit and stare and stare and sit Until they're hypnotised by it, Until they're absolutely drunk With all that shocking ghastly junk. Oh yes, we know it keeps them still, They don't climb out the window sill, They never fight or kick or punch, They leave you free to cook the lunch And wash the dishes in the sink - But did you ever stop to think, To wonder just exactly what This does to your beloved tot? IT ROTS THE SENSE IN THE HEAD! IT KILLS IMAGINATION DEAD! IT CLOGS AND CLUTTERS UP THE MIND! IT MAKES A CHILD SO DULL AND BLIND HE CAN NO LONGER UNDERSTAND A FANTASY, A FAIRYLAND! HIS BRAIN BECOMES AS SOFT AS CHEESE! HIS POWERS OF THINKING RUST AND FREEZE! HE CANNOT THINK - HE ONLY SEES! 'All right! ' you'll cry. 'All right! ' you'll say, 'But if we take the set away, What shall we do to entertain Our darling children? Please explain! ' We'll answer this by asking you, 'What used the darling ones to do? 'How used they keep themselves contented Before this monster was invented? ' Have you forgotten? Don't you know? We'll say it very loud and slow: THEY... USED... TO... READ! They'd READ and READ, AND READ and READ, and then proceed To READ some more. Great Scott! Gadzooks! One half their lives was reading books! The nursery shelves held books galore! Books cluttered up the nursery floor! And in the bedroom, by the bed, More books were waiting to be read! Such wondrous, fine, fantastic tales Of dragons, gypsies, queens, and whales And treasure isles, and distant shores Where smugglers rowed with muffled oars, And pirates wearing purple pants, And sailing ships and elephants, And cannibals crouching 'round the pot, Stirring away at something hot. (It smells so good, what can it be? Good gracious, it's Penelope.) The younger ones had Beatrix Potter With Mr. Tod, the dirty rotter, And Squirrel Nutkin, Pigling Bland, And Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle and- Just How The Camel Got His Hump, And How the Monkey Lost His Rump, And Mr. Toad, and bless my soul, There's Mr. Rat and Mr. Mole- Oh, books, what books they used to know, Those children living long ago! So please, oh please, we beg, we pray, Go throw your TV set away, And in its place you can install A lovely bookshelf on the wall. Then fill the shelves with lots of books, Ignoring all the dirty looks, The screams and yells, the bites and kicks, And children hitting you with sticks- Fear not, because we promise you That, in about a week or two Of having nothing else to do, They'll now begin to feel the need Of having something to read. And once they start - oh boy, oh boy! You watch the slowly growing joy That fills their hearts. They'll grow so keen They'll wonder what they'd ever seen In that ridiculous machine, That nauseating, foul, unclean, Repulsive television screen! And later, each and every kid Will love you more for what you did.

name_of_work: Where the Sidewalk Ends by Shel Silverstein
content: There is a place where the sidewalk ends And before the street begins, And there the grass grows soft and white, And there the sun burns crimson bright, And there the moon-bird rests from his flight To cool in the peppermint wind. Let us leave this place where the smoke blows black And the dark street winds and bends. Past the pits where the asphalt flowers grow We shall walk with a walk that is measured and slow, And watch where the chalk-white arrows go To the place where the sidewalk ends. Yes we'll walk with a walk that is measured and slow, And we'll go where the chalk-white arrows go, For the children, they mark, and the children, they know The place where the sidewalk ends.

Once upon a time, there was a charming little town. In the town, there was a big tunnel. The tunnel was dark and long. Many people went in and out of the tunnel every day.

One day, a little boy named Tim went into the tunnel. He wanted to see what was on the other side. Tim felt scared because it was so dark. But he was brave and kept going.

As Tim walked through the tunnel, he started to feel happy. He knew he was almost at the other end. When he came out of the tunnel, he saw a beautiful park. Tim played in the park all day and had lots of fun.

Once upon a time, there was a little duck named Ducky. Ducky loved to whistle while she waddled around the pond. One day, Ducky was feeling very hungry and wanted a snack. She looked around and saw a big, juicy worm wriggling in the mud. But Ducky didn't have any money to buy the worm because she was saving up for something special.

Suddenly, Ducky saw a sign that said "Cheap Snacks!" She was so excited and waddled over to see what they had. But when she got there, she saw that all the snacks were gone. Ducky was sad and hungry, but she didn't give up. She remembered that her friend, Mr. Frog, always had snacks. 

Ducky went to Mr. Frog's house and asked for a snack. Mr. Frog said he would give her one, but only if she could whistle a tune for him. Ducky tried to whistle, but she couldn't because she was too hungry. She remembered the worm and realized that if she ate it, she would have the energy to whistle. 

Ducky went back to the pond, ate the worm, and went back to Mr. Frog's house. She whistled a beautiful tune and Mr. Frog gave her a delicious snack. Ducky was happy and full, and she learned that sometimes you have to work hard to get what you want.

I've never, as some children do, looked at my folks and thought, I must have come from someone else -- rich parents who'd misplaced me, but who would, as in a myth or novel, return and claim me. Hell, no. I saw my face in cousins' faces, heard my voice in their high drawls. And Sundays, after the dinner plates were cleared, I lingered, elbow propped on red oilcloth, and studied great-uncles, aunts and cousins new to me. They squirmed. I stared till I discerned the features they'd gotten from the family larder: eyes, nose, lips, hair? I stared until, uncomfortable, they'd snap, "Hey, boy -- what are you looking at? At me?" "No, sir," I'd lie. "No, ma'am." I'd count ten and then continue staring at them. I never had to ask, What am I? I stared at my blood-kin, and thought, So this, dear God, is what I am.

Sara liked to make models with paper and glue. She cut the paper with scissors that were sharp. She was careful not to hurt herself or her friends. She made models of animals, houses, cars and flowers. She was very good at making models.

One day, she brought her models to school to show her teacher and her classmates. She was shy and did not like to talk much. She hoped they would like her models and say nice things. She put her models on a table in the corner of the room.

Tommy was a boy who liked to break things. He saw Sara's models and wanted to play with them. He did not ask Sara or the teacher. He grabbed a model of a car and threw it in the air. It fell on the floor and broke. Sara saw what Tommy did and felt sad. She ran to the table and tried to save her models.

"Stop it, Tommy! You are mean! You are breaking my models!" Sara shouted.

"I don't care. They are just paper. They are not fun. I want to see what is inside them." Tommy said. He picked up a model of a flower and ripped it apart. He saw the glue and the scissors that Sara used. He smiled and took the scissors.

Sara was scared. She knew the scissors were sharp and could hurt her or Tommy. She tried to take the scissors from Tommy, but he was stronger. He pushed her away and laughed. He waved the scissors in the air and said, "Look what I can do with these!"

He did not see the teacher coming behind him. The teacher saw the scissors and the broken models. She was angry and worried. She tried to grab the scissors from Tommy, but it was too late. Tommy moved the scissors too fast and cut the teacher's hand. The teacher screamed and blood came out. Tommy dropped the scissors and looked shocked. Sara cried and hugged her models. The teacher called for help and the other children ran away. It was a bad day.

My Soul, there is a country Afar beyond the stars, Where stands a winged sentry All skillful in the wars; There, above noise and danger Sweet Peace sits, crown'd with smiles, And One born in a manger Commands the beauteous files. He is thy gracious friend And (O my Soul awake!) Did in pure love descend, To die here for thy sake. If thou canst get but thither, There grows the flow'r of peace, The rose that cannot wither, Thy fortress, and thy ease. Leave then thy foolish ranges, For none can thee secure, But One, who never changes, Thy God, thy life, thy cure.

Sam and Tom are friends. They like to play with horses at the ranch. The ranch is a big place with many animals and plants. Sam and Tom help the rancher feed the horses and brush their fur.

One day, the rancher tells Sam and Tom that he has to separate some of the horses. He says that some horses are going to a new ranch far away. He says that they are very popular horses and many people want them.

Sam and Tom are sad. They do not want the horses to leave. They ask the rancher if they can say goodbye to the horses. The rancher says yes and takes them to the barn.

Sam and Tom hug and kiss their favorite horses. They tell them that they will miss them and that they are good horses. The horses neigh and nuzzle them. Sam and Tom feel happy and sad at the same time.

The rancher says that it is time to go. He thanks Sam and Tom for their help and says that they can come back anytime. He says that there are still many horses at the ranch that need their love and care. Sam and Tom smile and wave goodbye to the horses. They say that they will come back soon and that they will always be friends.

name_of_work: The Broken Tower by Hart Crane
content: The bell-rope that gathers God at dawn Dispatches me as though I dropped down the knell Of a spent day - to wander the cathedral lawn From pit to crucifix, feet chill on steps from hell. Have you not heard, have you not seen that corps Of shadows in the tower, whose shoulders sway Antiphonal carillons launched before The stars are caught and hived in the sun's ray? The bells, I say, the bells break down their tower; And swing I know not where. Their tongues engrave Membrane through marrow, my long-scattered score Of broken intervals... And I, their sexton slave! Oval encyclicals in canyons heaping The impasse high with choir. Banked voices slain! Pagodas, campaniles with reveilles out leaping- O terraced echoes prostrate on the plain!... And so it was I entered the broken world To trace the visionary company of love, its voice An instant in the wind (I know not whither hurled) But not for long to hold each desperate choice. My word I poured. But was it cognate, scored Of that tribunal monarch of the air Whose thigh embronzes earth, strikes crystal Word In wounds pledged once to hope - cleft to despair? The steep encroachments of my blood left me No answer (could blood hold such a lofty tower As flings the question true?) -or is it she Whose sweet mortality stirs latent power?- And through whose pulse I hear, counting the strokes My veins recall and add, revived and sure The angelus of wars my chest evokes: What I hold healed, original now, and pure... And builds, within, a tower that is not stone (Not stone can jacket heaven) - but slip Of pebbles, - visible wings of silence sown In azure circles, widening as they dip The matrix of the heart, lift down the eye That shrines the quiet lake and swells a tower... The commodious, tall decorum of that sky Unseals her earth, and lifts love in its shower.

Lila and Tom were playing on the sand. They liked to make castles and dig holes. They saw the big water that moved and made noise. It was the ocean. Lila wanted to go closer and touch it. Tom was scared.

"Come on, Tom, let's go see the water!" Lila said.

"No, Lila, it's too big and too loud. It might hurt us," Tom said.

Lila did not listen. She ran to the water and put her feet in. It was cold and wet. She laughed and splashed. Tom watched from the sand. He was worried.

Suddenly, a big wave came and knocked Lila down. She cried out and tried to get up. But the water was strong and pulled her in. She struggled and kicked. She was scared and hurt.

"Help, Tom, help!" she shouted.

Tom heard her and ran to the water. He was brave and grabbed her hand. He pulled and pulled. He struggled and shouted. He was scared and hurt too.

Finally, they got out of the water and fell on the sand. They were wet and cold and tired. They hugged each other and cried.

"Are you okay, Lila?" Tom asked.

"Yes, Tom, I'm okay. Thank you for saving me. You are a good brother," Lila said.

"I'm sorry, Lila, I was mean to you. I was just afraid of the water. It's too big and too loud for us. Let's stay on the sand and play," Tom said.

They nodded and smiled. They went back to their castles and holes. They were happy and safe. They learned to be careful of the ocean.

The cottage hearth beams warm and bright, The candles gaily glow; The stars emit a kinder light Above the drifted snow. Down from the sky a magic steals To glad the passing year, And belfries sing with joyous peals, For Christmastide is here!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to paint with her fingers and make pretty pictures. One day, her dad brought home a big machine that made loud noises. Lily was scared at first, but her dad showed her how the machine worked and she thought it was cool.

The next day, Lily decided to paint a picture of the cute animals she saw at the park. She used her fingers to make the animals and trees on the paper. She was so happy with her painting that she wanted to show her dad. But when she went to find him, he was using the big machine.

Lily watched as her dad used the machine to make something new. When he was finished, he showed her a cute toy he had made just for her. Lily was so happy and hugged her dad. She knew that even though the machine was loud and scary, it could also make cute things too.

A neighbourhood. At dusk. Things are getting ready to happen out of sight. Stars and moths. And rinds slanting around fruit. But not yet. One tree is black. One window is yellow as butter. A woman leans down to catch a child who has run into her arms this moment. Stars rise. Moths flutter. Apples sweeten in the dark.

I Like a gondola of green scented fruits Drifting along the dank canals of Venice, You, O exquisite one, Have entered into my desolate city. II The blue smoke leaps Like swirling clouds of birds vanishing. So my love leaps forth toward you, Vanishes and is renewed. III A rose-yellow moon in a pale sky When the sunset is faint vermilion In the mist among the tree-boughs Art thou to me, my beloved. IV A young beech tree on the edge of the forest Stands still in the evening, Yet shudders through all its leaves in the light air And seems to fear the stars-- So are you still and so tremble. V The red deer are high on the mountain, They are beyond the last pine trees. And my desires have run with them. VI The flower which the wind has shaken Is soon filled again with rain; So does my heart fill slowly with tears, O Foam-Driver, Wind-of-the-Vineyards, Until you return.

Ben and Lily liked to play with their toy rocket. They pretended it could fly to the moon and the stars. They made zoom and blast sounds with their mouths.

One day, they found a big box in the garage. It had a picture of a real rocket on it. Ben and Lily were very excited. They opened the box and saw a beautiful rocket inside. It was shiny and red and had a window and a door.

"Wow, look at this rocket!" Ben said. "Can we play with it, please?"

Lily nodded. "Yes, let's play with it. Maybe we can go to space!"

They lifted the rocket out of the box and carried it to the backyard. They put it on the grass and climbed inside. They closed the door and looked out the window.

"Ready for takeoff?" Ben asked.

"Ready!" Lily said.

They pushed some buttons and pulled some levers. The rocket made a loud noise and started to shake.

"Yield, yield, yield!" Lily shouted. "What does that mean?"

Ben looked at a flashing light on the dashboard. It said "yield". He did not know what it meant. He thought it was a warning.

"Maybe it means we have to stop," he said. "Maybe the rocket is broken."

He pushed another button and the noise stopped. The rocket stopped shaking.

They opened the door and got out of the rocket. They saw their dad coming from the garage. He looked angry.

"Ben, Lily, what are you doing with my rocket?" he asked. "This is not a toy. This is a model rocket for my hobby. You could have hurt yourselves or damaged the rocket. Yield means you have to wait for a signal before you launch it. You have to be careful and follow the rules."

Ben and Lily felt sorry. They did not mean to upset their dad. They liked the rocket, but they did not know it was not a toy.

"We're sorry, dad," they said. "We just wanted to play with the rocket. It's so beautiful. Can we watch you launch it someday?"

Their dad sighed. He was not happy, but he loved his children. He hugged them and said, "Maybe someday, when you're older and you learn more about rockets. But for now, you have to play with your toy rocket. It's safer and more fun. And you have to ask me before you touch anything in the garage. OK?"

Ben and Lily nodded. They said, "OK, dad. We understand. We love you."

They took their toy rocket and went back to their room. They still dreamed of going to space, but they knew they had to wait and learn. They played with their toy rocket and had fun. They made zoom and blast sounds with their mouths.

name_of_work: In drear-nighted December by John Keats
content: In drear nighted December, Too happy, happy tree, Thy branches ne'er remember Their green felicity-- The north cannot undo them With a sleety whistle through them Nor frozen thawings glue them From budding at the prime. In drear-nighted December, Too happy, happy brook, Thy bubblings ne'er remember Apollo's summer look; But with a sweet forgetting, They stay their crystal fretting, Never, never petting About the frozen time. Ah! would 'twere so with many A gentle girl and boy-- But were there ever any Writh'd not of passed joy? The feel of not to feel it, When there is none to heal it Nor numbed sense to steel it, Was never said in rhyme.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to smell flowers and make pretty things. One day, Lily's mom brought home a bottle of perfume. It smelled really good! Lily was glad and sprayed some on her wrist. She liked it so much that she recommended it to her friends at preschool. They all wanted to smell like flowers too! So, Lily's mom bought more perfume and gave it to all of her friends. They were all glad and smelled really nice. The end.

Tim and Sam are brothers. They like to play with cars and trucks. One day, they find a big red truck in the garage. It is their dad's truck. They want to drive it.

"Let's start the truck!" Tim says. He climbs into the driver's seat. He puts the key in the hole and turns it.

"No, Tim, stop!" Sam says. He is scared. He knows they are not allowed to touch the truck. "Dad will be mad!"

But Tim is stubborn. He does not listen to Sam. He pushes the pedal and the truck moves. It goes fast and loud. It hits the wall and makes a big hole. Tim and Sam are hurt. They cry.

Dad hears the noise and runs to the garage. He sees the truck and the hole and his sons. He is very angry and sad. He yells at Tim and Sam. He takes them to the doctor. He says they are in big trouble. They have to pay for the damage. They have to say sorry. They have to learn to obey.

Tim and Sam are sorry. They wish they had listened to Sam. They wish they had not started the truck. They have learned a hard lesson. They have a bad ending.

HE'D have given me rolling lands, Houses of marble, and billowing farms, Pearls, to trickle between my hands, Smoldering rubies, to circle my arms. You--you'd only a lilting song, Only a melody, happy and high, You were sudden and swift and strong,-- Never a thought for another had I. He'd have given me laces rare, Dresses that glimmered with frosty sheen, Shining ribbons to wrap my hair, Horses to draw me, as fine as a queen. You--you'd only to whistle low, Gaily I followed wherever you led. I took you, and I let him go,-- Somebody ought to examine my head!

name_of_work: And Death Shall Have No Dominion by Dylan Thomas
content: And death shall have no dominion. Dead men naked they shall be one With the man in the wind and the west moon; When their bones are picked clean and the clean bones gone, They shall have stars at elbow and foot; Though they go mad they shall be sane, Though they sink through the sea they shall rise again; Though lovers be lost love shall not; And death shall have no dominion. And death shall have no dominion. Under the windings of the sea They lying long shall not die windily; Twisting on racks when sinews give way, Strapped to a wheel, yet they shall not break; Faith in their hands shall snap in two, And the unicorn evils run them through; Split all ends up they shan't crack; And death shall have no dominion. And death shall have no dominion. No more may gulls cry at their ears Or waves break loud on the seashores; Where blew a flower may a flower no more Lift its head to the blows of the rain; Though they be mad and dead as nails, Heads of the characters hammer through daisies; Break in the sun till the sun breaks down, And death shall have no dominion.

Once upon a time, there was a stubborn oak tree. The tree guarded a special flag. The flag waved proudly in the wind.

Every morning, the flag greeted the sun with a big smile. Everyone in the town was so happy to see it.

But one day, a mean woodcutter tried to take the flag away. The woodcutter had a big saw and was determined to get the flag.

But the stubborn oak tree wouldn't let him. He shook his branches to prevent the woodcutter from getting close. The woodcutter poked and prodded but the tree was too strong.

In the end, the woodcutter had to give up. The flag stayed safe and could greet the sun every morning. Everyone in the town was so pleased that the stubborn oak tree had prevented the woodcutter from taking away their flag.

The sun was shining hot on the garden. Mira saw an old rake in the grass. She picked it up and started playing with it.

Mira's mom saw her and said, "Mira, why don't you rake the garden, so the it becomes nice and tidy."

Mira looked around and saw the grass growing wild. She began raking vigorously. She gathered the dry leaves and the disgusting weeds.

When Mira had finished, her Mom said, "I'm so proud of you, Mira. You have healed the garden!"

Mira was so excited. She smiled and hugged her Mom. From then on, Mira enjoyed taking care of the garden.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She lived in a big house with her mommy and daddy. Lily loved to play with her toys upstairs.

One day, Lily's mommy said, "Lily, hurry! We need to go shopping." Lily didn't want to stop playing, but she knew she had to listen to her mommy. So, she put her toys away and went downstairs.

On the way to the store, Lily saw a tough-looking dog. The dog was big and barked loudly. Lily wanted to pet the dog, but her mommy said, "No, Lily. That dog might not be friendly."

Lily didn't listen to her mommy and went to pet the dog anyway. The tough dog bit Lily's hand, and she cried. Her mommy took her to the doctor to make her feel better.

The moral of the story is to always listen to your mommy and daddy, because they know what's best for you.

The little girl was ready to go outside. She was very excited! She opened the door and stepped out into the dark night. The moon was shining above her, so she decided to gaze up at it. As she looked up at the sky, she saw a figure in the distance. She was scared but she couldn't turn away. The figure crept closer and closer. Suddenly it lunged forward, ready to grab her. She screamed and ran back inside. She never gazed up at the sky again.

Once upon a time, there was a little fish named Nemo. Nemo loved to swim and play with his fish friends. One day, Nemo wanted to play hide and seek. He hid behind a rock and waited for his friends to find him. 

But Nemo was not successful in hiding. His bright orange color made him easy to spot. His friends found him quickly and laughed. Nemo felt sad and embarrassed. 

Nemo's mom saw him and asked what was wrong. Nemo told her what happened. His mom said, "Nemo, it's okay if you're not successful at hiding. What's important is that you had fun playing with your friends. And remember, it's not about winning or losing, it's about having fun and being kind to others." 

Nemo felt better and realized his mom was right. He went back to playing with his friends, happy and carefree. The end.

Once upon a time there were two friends, Jack and Jill. They lived near a river and loved to play there.

One day they were in the river playing, when they started to quarrel. They shouted at each other and splashed the dull water everywhere. 

Jack wanted to keep playing, but Jill didn't. She was annoyed and wanted to go home. No matter how hard Jack tried to get her to stay, she refused to listen.

So eventually they both left in a huff, and Jill walked away in tears. Jack felt sad, because he didn't want to quarrel with his friend.

Then something amazing happened. Jack suddenly noticed a little boat in the side of the river. It was a beautiful boat, with shiny sails and bright colors.

Jack shouted for Jill to stop and he showed her the boat. Jill's eyes sparkled and she quickly forgot about their quarrel. They both raced inside and sailed away in the boat.

The boat carried them far away, to an amazing place filled with wonders. They were never sad again, and their friendship was stronger than ever.

Lily and Ben are friends. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a big dog with a spike on his collar. The dog is barking loud.

"Wow, look at that dog!" Ben says. "He has a spike. He looks scary."

Lily is not afraid. She likes dogs. She walks to the dog and says, "Hello, dog. What is your name?"

The dog stops barking. He wags his tail. He says, "My name is Rex. I am a gifted dog. I can talk."

Lily and Ben are surprised. They have never heard a dog talk before.

"You can talk?" Lily asks. "How can you do that?"

Rex says, "I learned from my owner. He is a scientist. He gave me a special chip in my ear. It helps me understand and speak human words."

Lily and Ben think that is amazing. They want to learn more about Rex and his owner. They ask Rex if they can play with him.

Rex says, "Sure, I like to play. But be careful of my spike. It is sharp. It is for protection."

Lily and Ben nod. They pet Rex gently. They play fetch and tag with him. They have a lot of fun.

Rex is happy. He likes Lily and Ben. He thinks they are gifted too. They are kind and curious. He says, "You are my new friends. Do you want to come to my home and meet my owner?"

Lily and Ben say, "Yes, please. We would love to meet him."

They follow Rex to his home. They are excited to see what other surprises he has. They think Rex is a very special dog.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to explore the big city with her mommy. They would walk around and see all the tall buildings and busy people.

One day, Lily saw a man who looked sad. She asked her mommy, "Why is that man sad?" Her mommy replied, "Maybe something disturbed him."

Lily wanted to help the man feel better, so she gave him a useful toy that she had in her pocket. The man smiled and said, "Thank you, little girl. You made my day better."

Lily felt happy that she could make someone smile. From that day on, she always brought a useful toy with her when she explored the city with her mommy.

"Look, I have a new book!" said Ben. He ran to his shelf and took a book with a brown cover. It had a picture of a mule on it. "Do you know what a mule is?" he asked Lily.

Lily shook her head. She had never seen a mule before. Ben opened the book and pointed to the mule. "A mule is a kind of animal. It has four legs and a long nose. It can carry heavy things on its back. It is very powerful."

"Wow, a mule is amazing!" said Lily. She wanted to print a mule too. She took a brown crayon and tried to copy the picture from the book. She drew a big body, four legs, a long nose, and two ears. She was very proud of her print.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play with his toy weapons and pretend he was a superhero. One day, Timmy was playing with his toys outside when his friend Billy came over.

"Wow, Timmy! I admire your cool toy sword," said Billy, who was enthusiastic about playing with Timmy.

"Thanks, Billy! Do you want to play superheroes with me?" asked Timmy.

"Sure, but can I borrow your toy weapon?" asked Billy.

"Of course! Here you go," said Timmy, handing Billy the toy sword.

Timmy and Billy played together for hours, fighting imaginary villains and saving the day. They both had so much fun and were very enthusiastic about playing together. At the end of the day, they both went home with big smiles on their faces, already planning their next adventure.

Once there was a girl called Amy. She was an impatient three year old. She had a problem and didn't know what to do. Then something amazing happened!

Amy's uncle came to visit. He was very kind. Amy told him her problem. Her uncle listened carefully and thought of a way to solve it.

Amy was so glad that her uncle had come to visit! She was no longer worried. With the help of her uncle, she soon solved the problem.

Amy was very happy. She thanked her uncle for helping her and she was no longer impatient. She knew she could count on her uncle if ever she needed help again.

Rico had been waiting for his haircut for weeks. He loved his long hair and was very excited for the day to come. His little sister Gracie, who was three years old, was jealous of the haircut and wanted one as well.

When the day arrived, Rico and Gracie went to the barbershop together. Gracie looked around nervously as she saw all the big chairs and mirrors. Rico was not nervous at all and held her little hand tightly. 

When it was time for Rico's haircut, the barber began to work. But... Rico was worried. He did not want Gracie to feel left out and he wanted to make sure she would have fun too.

He stopped the barber and asked, "Can Gracie have a haircut too?" The barber was shocked, but understood his request. He gave Rico a very special haircut and then cut Gracie's hair too. Gracie's hair had been so filthy and untidy, but after the haircut it was neat and shiny.

Gracie and Rico were so excited about their new haircuts. They had so much fun together, and it was an unforgettable experience for them. The children thanked the barber for understanding their special request, and the barber smiled. He loved that the siblings could share in this experience.

name_of_work: The Ballad of the Harp-Weaver by Edna St. Vincent Millay
content: "Son," said my mother, When I was knee-high, "You've need of clothes to cover you, And not a rag have I. "There's nothing in the house To make a boy breeches, Nor shears to cut a cloth with Nor thread to take stitches. "There's nothing in the house But a loaf-end of rye, And a harp with a woman's head Nobody will buy," And she began to cry. That was in the early fall. When came the late fall, "Son," she said, "the sight of you Makes your mother's blood crawl,-- "Little skinny shoulder-blades Sticking through your clothes! And where you'll get a jacket from God above knows. "It's lucky for me, lad, Your daddy's in the ground, And can't see the way I let His son go around!" And she made a queer sound. That was in the late fall. When the winter came, I'd not a pair of breeches Nor a shirt to my name. I couldn't go to school, Or out of doors to play. And all the other little boys Passed our way. "Son," said my mother, "Come, climb into my lap, And I'll chafe your little bones While you take a nap." And, oh, but we were silly For half an hour or more, Me with my long legs Dragging on the floor, A-rock-rock-rocking To a mother-goose rhyme! Oh, but we were happy For half an hour's time! But there was I, a great boy, And what would folks say To hear my mother singing me To sleep all day, In such a daft way? Men say the winter Was bad that year; Fuel was scarce, And food was dear. A wind with a wolf's head Howled about our door, And we burned up the chairs And sat on the floor. All that was left us Was a chair we couldn't break, And the harp with a woman's head Nobody would take, For song or pity's sake. The night before Christmas I cried with the cold, I cried myself to sleep Like a two-year-old. And in the deep night I felt my mother rise, And stare down upon me With love in her eyes. I saw my mother sitting On the one good chair, A light falling on her From I couldn't tell where, Looking nineteen, And not a day older, And the harp with a woman's head Leaned against her shoulder. Her thin fingers, moving In the thin, tall strings, Were weav-weav-weaving Wonderful things. Many bright threads, From where I couldn't see, Were running through the harp-strings Rapidly, And gold threads whistling Through my mother's hand. I saw the web grow, And the pattern expand. She wove a child's jacket, And when it was done She laid it on the floor And wove another one. She wove a red cloak So regal to see, "She's made it for a king's son," I said, "and not for me." But I knew it was for me. She wove a pair of breeches Quicker than that! She wove a pair of boots And a little cocked hat. She wove a pair of mittens, She wove a little blouse, She wove all night In the still, cold house. She sang as she worked, And the harp-strings spoke; Her voice never faltered, And the thread never broke. And when I awoke,-- There sat my mother With the harp against her shoulder Looking nineteen And not a day older, A smile about her lips, And a light about her head, And her hands in the harp-strings Frozen dead. And piled up beside her And toppling to the skies, Were the clothes of a king's son, Just my size.

Lily and Ben were best friends. They liked to play in the park every day. They had a secret spot under a big tree, where they hid their toys and snacks. They always held hands when they crossed the street.

One day, Lily's mom said they had to move to a new house far away. Lily was very sad. She wanted to stay with Ben. She told Ben the bad news. Ben was sad too. He said, "I will miss you, Lily. You are my best friend. Can we still talk on the phone?"

Lily nodded. She said, "Yes, we can. And we can write letters and draw pictures. And maybe we can visit each other someday. But we have to remember each other, Ben. Promise me you will remember me."

Ben promised. He said, "I will remember you, Lily. You are my best friend. I will never forget you." They hugged and kissed. They said goodbye.

The next day, Lily and her mom left for the new house. Lily looked out the window and saw Ben waving at her. She waved back. She held her hand to her heart. She said, "I will remember you, Ben."

But Lily did not remember Ben. She made new friends in the new house. She played with new toys and ate new snacks. She forgot about the park and the tree and the phone and the letters and the pictures. She forgot about Ben.

And Ben did not remember Lily. He made new friends in the park. He played with new toys and ate new snacks. He forgot about the house and the window and the phone and the letters and the pictures. He forgot about Lily.

They never saw each other again. They never talked to each other again. They never remembered each other again. They were not best friends anymore.

Once there was a little girl called Anna. She was very troubled and often felt alone. One day, Anna asked her mum for a story. Her mum said she was too busy. Anna felt so sad but she decided not to get angry and instead ignore her mum.

Anna went outside to play. She was still feeling troubled but wanted to stay happy. She saw a big, strong tree beside the house. She decided to climb it and look out over the garden.

As Anna climbed higher and higher, she heard a noise from a branch above her. A little bird had been hiding there and was very scared at being disturbed. Anna smiled and decided to ignore the bird, so it would feel more at ease.

Soon the bird stopped being scared and started to make lovely chirpy noises. Anna laughed with joy and she felt much better then before. She waved goodbye to the bird and climbed down from the tree.

It was time for bed and Anna's troubles were gone. She dreams of her special tree and knew that everything will be alright.

Once upon a time, there was a poor cat. She was so itchy that she couldn't bear it any longer! She meowed loudly and started scratching herself all over.

Suddenly, a small mouse peeked out of its hole. "What is happening?" he asked.

The cat meowed sadly and said, "I'm so itchy and poor. I need help!"

The mouse was very kind. He said, "My friend the owl can help. Let me go and ask him to listen."

The mouse ran to the owl's tree. He explained the cat's problem, and the owl said he could help.

The owl flew back with the mouse and said to the cat, "Listen carefully. I know the remedy for itchy skin. If you eat this, your itch will go away."

The cat thanked the owl and ate the remedy. She felt much better immediately. 

"Thank you so much, kind friends," she said.

The mouse and the owl smiled and said, "You're welcome!"

One morning, a curious three year old hopped out of bed, eager for an adventurous day. She decided she would wander around her house, to see what there was to discover. As she mad her way down the hallway, she spotted something in front of her. It was a shiny eye attached to a string! She had never seen anything like it before. She was so curious and wanted to explore more, so she followed the string around the corner.

The little girl wandered through the house, and each corner seemed more exciting than the last. She felt so brave and daring, following the eye and winding string around. She went up the stairs, and under the table, she stopped to observe the eye. It had a bright blue stone in the middle that seemed to sparkle in the morning sun!

The little one wandered around and around the house, the eye and string guiding her way. Eventually, she found herself back downstairs and hummed a happy song, proud of her adventurous morning. She had seen so much and had so much fun. 

The little girl smiled and placed the eye back where she found it, satisfied with her discovery. She skipped back to her room, excited to tell her parents all about her morning!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a brother named Max who was very big and strong. Max liked to sit on the couch and watch TV all day. One day, Lily wanted to show Max how graceful she could be. She put on her favorite dress and started dancing around the living room. Max watched her dance and was amazed by how graceful she was. He even got up from the couch and started dancing with her. From that day on, Max didn't just sit on the couch all day. He started dancing with Lily and they had lots of fun together. The end.

name_of_work: The Poem as Mask by Muriel Rukeyser
content: Orpheus When I wrote of the women in their dances and wildness, it was a mask, on their mountain, god-hunting, singing, in orgy, it was a mask; when I wrote of the god, fragmented, exiled from himself, his life, the love gone down with song, it was myself, split open, unable to speak, in exile from myself. There is no mountain, there is no god, there is memory of my torn life, myself split open in sleep, the rescued child beside me among the doctors, and a word of rescue from the great eyes. No more masks! No more mythologies! Now, for the first time, the god lifts his hand, the fragments join in me with their own music.
